The sudden throwing up of his lecture engage- ments by Dr. Nansen is regarded as meaning that he was not having the reception he expected, and that the interest manifested was insufficient. Any- one who has lectured in America has the same kind of story to tell. At some places the excitement is acute and overwhelming,and at others the audience seems ignorant, frigid, and depressed. The proba- bility is that Dr. Nansen was to well reported to make heavy draws possible in some places. Arctic questions, moreover, have had a pretty good run, but excitement about them has its limits. If Dr. Nansen goes with Peary on another expedition he may revive public interest.

Signs multiply, in the papers and in club con- versations, that a change is coming over men's minds respecting the forward frontier policy. It is no longer defended with warmth. It is no longer heresy to question the dictum of this or that mili- tary authority. The matter is viewed in the light of facts. The policy has led to disaster from the time surrender was. made to it, and the story is being retold in many ways. Military men are by no means reluctant to condemn where they formerly approved, and politicians are constrained to admit that a mistake was made in August, 1895, from which we are suffering now.

The Progressive party in London ' have decided not to invite the assistance of the leaders of the Liberal party in the fierce fight which is about to Ibe waged for the control of the London County Council. The Moderates, on the other hand, will have the assistance of Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Bal- four,and other front-benchers of the Unionist party. , This decision of the Progressive party will not ex- I elude Lord Rosebery, whose withdrawal from the leadership of the Liberal party does not affect the position he gained for himself by his early labours as Chairman of the London County Council. Lord Rosebery is expected to take a prominent part in the campaign and there will be a certain interest in the spectacle of the late Liberal chief leading al- most single-banded the democratic forces of Lon- don against the combined forces of municipal sad Imperial reaction, whilst his late Parliamentary col- leagues stand aside.

Or. Jameson bas not received any lionising since his arrival in the metropolis, and he has not laid himself out for it. Only the solicitor to the Char- tered Company and some enterprising newspaper re- porter seemed to remember that he was coming to this country. Two years ago, as the hero of the raid, he had to be smugglscl into court by round- about routes, and be became the cynosure of many fair and admiring eyes at Bow-street and elsewhere, and also a hero of the crowd. .Now he disappears as it were into space,with the intimation that he is going into the country, and then to the Continent. The world troubles itself about him ne further. ITimes are changed. but I admire his modesty.

The discussions on Vie condition of parties at Birmingham are most amusing in their variety and inconclusiveness, and Mr. Chamberlain is being highly praised for his tact and resourcefulness by exactly the Pereone who know least about the true state of affairs. The discontent which exists turns upon educational policy more than anything else, and it seems likely to go on simmering for some time. I am in constant touch with some of the wirepulling fraternity in Birmingham. and I find them all agreed that the pres-mt discontent is much more serious than is known to the world. But then they are equally agreed thst Mr. Cham- berlain cannot help bh.self. Offile constrains him to give up what he would have retained had he been a free agent.

Wednesday was the Marquis of Salisbury's birth- day. He was sixty-eight Be looks more, and since he has begun to stoop so much other symp- toms of advancing years are evident. But in his general physical health he has nothing to complain of just now,and his drowsihess from which be suf- fered two or three months ago has disappeared. The current gossip about some insidious malady from which he suffers is all nonsense. Any insurance office would take his life for another ten years at any rate,though the Cecils do not as a rule live over seventy-five or seventy-six.

His state has been the subject ef much sympathetic talk in the club, and every edition of the evening papers has been eagerly scanned for the latest news regarding his progress.

One thing appears to have been pretty well es- tablished of late in the minds of most persons, and that is the impossibility of trusting to declarations about foreign affairs made by members of the Government who are not in the Cabinet. They are behind in their news,they exaggerate any decisions which may have been come to, and they do not know more than the intelligent outsider. Sir It. Webster's recent remarks are cited as illustrative of this new position. He sina,Ay talked after the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and that is what any supporter of the Government could do without be- ing connected with the Administration.

UNE IN TEN THOUSAND.—SimpFon : "Jones has more self-restraint than any other man I know," Thompson: "Has he?" Simpson : " Yes ; he advised me not to buy that stock, and when he learned afterwards that I had dropped a thou- sand on it he never made the slightest allusion to the matter." PROBABLY.—Jones (just introduced) : "I suppose you don't remember me, but I was once a witness against your side in a certain trial, and I remember that you cross-examined me with the greatest courtesy." The Lawyer : "Is that so ! Perhaps your testimony was not material!' IN Australia the cyclist seems to be, even more than with us, the master of the situation. Wit- ness the "Hints to Pedestrians," published by the League of Victorian Whcelmen : Never walk on a footpath—you may overturn a cyclist. Never cross a road—you may damage a costly machine. Never travel on the dummy—it distracts the atten- tion of the wheelmen ridivg alongside. When you see a bicycle coming—climb a tree. " WELL, here is the money you've been torment- ing me for," said a rich uncle to his spendthrift nephew. " Uae it wisely, and remember that a fool and his money are soon parted." "I don't 1:11-,Av aly,ut that," replied the young scrapegrace. '"l've been coaxing you more than a week for this."

AN INTELLIGENT WITNESS. —A witness in court who had been cautioned to give a precise answer to every question, and not to talk about what he might think the question meant, was interro- gated as follows : " You drive a waggon?" "No, sir, I do not." "Why, sir, did you not tell my learned friend so this moment?" "No, sir, I did not.' "Now, sir, I put is to you on your oath. Do you drive a waggon ?" "No, sir." " What is your occupation, then?" "I drive a horse." THE BICYCLE EYE.—The bicycle will soon affect the entire human race. The bicycle face has been exploited and observed until everybody is familiar with the wild and forlorn anguish of its expression. But now we have the bicycle eye. From the nervous tension, and the necessity of constantly watching for stones, ditches and tramcars, the eyes .of the confirmed bicyclist are slowly starting from their sockets. Every year will add to this deformity until before long we may expect to see the eyes of mankind constructed on the same principle as those of the snail—removed to quite a distance from the head. This condition will make the use of spectacles very inconvenient, and will make winking a very laborious and grotesque perform- -once, if not absolutely impossible. WHAT TO CULTIVATE.—" If a girl is anxious to marry"— began the maid. " Yes ? " said the woman of the world, encouragingly. "If she is anxious to marry and marry well from the point of view of Society, I suppose she should prepare herself as she would for a profession." "Certainly." "The are some things thrit she should cultivate assiduously, and others to %%bleb she need devote little attention." " There are." " Well, what would you advise her to cultivate particularly?" " A wealthy relative who is likely to die soon." . . . . .

WHICH ?—The following story is told in tilitagow , University about Professors Gaud and Sir William Thomson (now Lord Kelvin). On one occasion the professors were under the necessity of personally conducting a student, who had become suddenly insane, to a neighbouring lunatic asylum in the small hours of the morning. On arriving at the asylum, their application for admission was answered by an attendant, who inquired from a second-storey window who they were. "Pro- fessors Caird and Thomson," they replied. " Ah," queried the attendant, "which of you has brought the other?" THE cook came upstairs, and twisting up the -corner of her apron with considerable embarrass- ment, said to her mistress: "You. see, minis, I thought it mought be bes' to be tellm' you dat—dat I done got married las' week." " Ah, indeed! And what is your name now, Hannah ? " me Williams, ma'am. You see, my husban' he sin a • cook, too. He am what dey calls a sheft in a hotel." "A chef, heh ? That's very nice. And do you expect to leave us directly, Hannah?" "Not d'rectly, mum. I'll stay wid ye for de present. You see my husban's he's done gone to New York an' Washington on his honeymoon, an' it'll be nigh on to six weeks befo' he comes back 1" HAD LEARNT THE LESSON.—The son was about to enter upon the sea of matrimony. The father called him to his side, and give him a final lesson in economy. "Economy," said the father, "is the source of all wealth, and extravagance is the ruination of genius. "Now," continued the parent, "a woman can take a piece of 5"8•W, trim it, and it will be a guinea hat. On the worrian's part that is —? " "Genius," the son answ•;red. " A wealthy man can expend £2,000 a year, and live no better than the man that spends only £2OO. On the wealthy man's part that's--? " "Extrava- gance." "Now to the point. A married man can live on one half the money,that a single man requires. On the married man's part that's—?" Com- pulsory." A DETERMINED MALINGERER. —ln a hotel in New York there was a night watchman who did not take kindly to the system requiring him to go through the hotel at certain hours and touch electric buttons fitted up in various places. After much thought he fired up an automat Jo arrangement on several of the buttons, so that they would report -at certain hours. Soon the button system got so out of order that the management had it taken out. •It was found necessary to keep watch in some way on the watchman, however, and finally a pedometer was given him to carry on his rounds which would register every step he took. All went well the first two nights thereafter, but on the morning following the third night the old man was missing. On search being made he was found sound asleep in the engine-room, and the pedometer so attached to the piston-rod of tha engine that worked the electric light that with every stroke it registered a step. It had been travelling all night, and when i taken off t registered two hundred and ,twelve miles.

div.head: FOLLY POINT.
div.p: THE FOLLY POINT.

MIDWAY between Bewdley and Arley, lies a cottage snugly ensconced on the banks of the Severn, in which the three persons concerned in this sketch reside. The spot is called " The Folly Point," and is well-known to thousands of tourists. The cottage is occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Masser an family. Mr. and Mrs Masser are people of middle age ; the husband is connected with the Kinlet Colliery, three miles away,and his wife, a buxom matron, is the mother of three children, two of whom attend the school at Trimpley. A representative of the Kidderminster Times paid a visit quite unexpectedly to "Folly Point," andinter- viewed the occupants of the cottage. When the object of the writer's visit was made known to Mrs. Maeser,she at once related the following : "1 had suffered for five years with a burning sensa- tion in my stomach, which was always with me—night and day, and after trying almost everything without any benefit, I went to the hospital at West Bromwich for treatment, knowing that the best medical treatment Is always to he had at hospitals. I was treated there for 1 SIX months, but received no benefit. I then consulted 1 several eminent doctors for advice, but none of them seemed to do me good- My husband advised me to write to Dr. Williams' Company describing my complaint, and to ask if their pills would be likely to de me any good. On receiving a reply in the affirmative I then bought a hex of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People at Bridg- north. When I returned home I thought I was dying- -80 great was the pain all over me—and I then took one of the pills, which seemed to do me good at once. I kept on taking them—three times a day—and after two boxes I found myself really much better, with the pain in my stomiteh quite gone. The burning sensation had left me ; and I now feel better than for many a year past. I feel certain that if I had not-taken the pills in time I should not be alive W. Now my husband and my little girl, nine years old, at school at Trimpley, are taking them." Mrs. Masser went on to say she wed to suffer from sick headache, but had never experienced the sickly sen- sation since she had been in the habit of taking Dr. Wil- liams' Pills. Her little girl was thrown down at school, and had her hip diseased. Now she's at school at Trim- pley, two miles away, and is only able to walk the dis- tance through taking Dr. Williams' Pills. " For some time," said Mrs. Masser, "she was quite a cripple, and when I wrote to Dr. Williams' Company I asked also if the pills would do her any good. They certainly have done her good, for she can play and jump and go about everywhere now. She goes to school regularly, and I expect, as I continue the pills, they'll quite cure her. My husband suffered a great deal from sickness in the morning, and hated the sight of food, but after a time he was persuaded to try Dr. Williams' Pink Pills, and his appetite is as good as ever it was. A neighbour of Mine at Erdington said to me one day, Mrs. Masser, YOU look a lot better,' and I said, 'Yes, I have been tak- ing Dr. Williams' Pink Pills.' She suffered too, and said 'Do you think they would do me any good ?' and I said, ' Well, they have cured me--what no doctor could do.' Well, the end silt was that she started taking the pills, and the last time I saw her she said the pills had done her more good than all the footers, and I could see a marked improvement in her appearance." Mrs. Masser's account of these circunistancea bears weight, coming from a person of her intellect and*posi- tion. Dr. Williams' Pink Pills have more patrons among educated people and the clergy than any other medicine, because the proprietors are always willing to state with equal candour whether they have cured a given ailment or not. Anyone may write to the Company freely and at length, These pills have cured paralysis, locomotor ataxy, rheumatism, sciatica, and the after-effects ef in- finenzataleo all diseases arising/from the impoverishment of the blood, scrofula, rickets, chronic erysipelas, con- sumption of the newels and lunge, sweetie, pale and sallow complexion, general muscular weakness, loss of appetite, palpitations, pains in the back, nervous head- ache and neuralgia, early decay, all forms of female weakness, and hysteria. These Pills are a tonic, not a purgative. They are genuine only with the full name, Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and are sold by chemists and Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, 46, Hol- born Viaduct, London, EQ., at 2s. 9cl. a box, or six boxes for 13. 91. Pink Pills sold loose or from glass jars are not Dr.Willianne.

The Earl of Ava, Lord Duffnin's son, and Mr. C. Barine are reported from New York, where they have recently been staying,to be on their way to Klondike or its neighbourhood, in connection with a mining scheme in which the Duke of Teck.the Marquis of Dufferin, Mr. Ogden Mills, and other prominent men are said to be in- terested. The organisation of this Scheme,it is reported, has been in consideration for more than a year, but the Klondike discoveries are said to !vivo " lw.stened its emmuturnation."

div.p: rHE EXAIVIINER FRIDAY. FEBII' 'Ala 4 1898.
BERYL'S HUSBAND, • BY MRS. HARRIET LEWIS, AUTHOR OF °Darkwood," "Lady Kildare," " &Indere,. Hearts,' "Her Double Life," &c.
CHAPTER XLVII. THE DAWN.

As the three gentlemen came in, Octavia strut; gled to her feet, and gasping for breath, sank int 4, a chair. Conyers and Callender still stood as it transfixed. The three conspirators could nm accept absolute ruin without a struggle. They were overwhelmed by the turn affairs had taken. They seemed too utterly stupified and bewildered to obey Lord Hawkhurst's command, but some vague thought of attempting to retrieve themselves by denials and protestations had already entered their minds. The earl resumed his seat. Mr. Sherwald, after a rapid, observant glance about the apartment, approached his lordship, with a countenance upon which a sense of relief was depicted. "I am glad to see you so much better, my Lord," he said. "I called yesterday and saw Mrs. Conyers, but she would not allow me to come in. She said that you were at the point of death and quite past attending to business." _ Sherwald's dislike to Octavia showed itself

plainly in this speech, which was, nevertheless, like all his utterances, literally true. "Mrs. Conyers has been very officious, but all that is over now. How do you do, Desmond? Glad to see you." Desmond advanced and shook hands with his august kinsman. "My lord, permit me to present to you Mr. Star, of Starwood, Surrey," said Sherwald. "I have brought him here to-day for a purpose which I will explain later." The earl blanched a little, but greeted Mr. Star politely. A single glance at the grim-faced farmer elicited the fact that the latter had not come to Hawkhurst House with any sinister designs against its owner.

"Be seated, sir," said Lord Hawkhurst. "Sit down, Desmond. I was about to send a messenger for you. Sherwald, did you bring the draft of the new will I ordered drawn up ?" " Y es, my lord, but—" "Give it to me.''

Sherwald drew a thin leathern envelope from his pocket, and produced from its inclosure the document in question. The earl opened it, and glanced over its contents. Then he laid it on the fire. It blazed up and vanished. "So perish my intention of making Rollyn Con yers my heir," said the earl, in aloud voice. "He will never inherit one penny of my estates I" Octavia began to sob violently. Conyers said not a word. The earl turned toward Desmond with an eager questioning face. "Have you found Mrs. Desmond yet?" he asked.

"No, my lord," said Desmond, anxiously. "We traced her to a house at Bayswater, but she got away in disguise and eluded us. We have searched everywhere, but are still hopeful. We are sure that we saw her yesterday." "So late as yesterday ?" exclaimed the earl. "I was in hopes that she was found already, but I am sure that she soon must be. Sherwald, no stone must be left unturned in the search for her I"

"None shall be, my lord. Mr. Desmond went down into Surrey and found Mr. Star, who is the uncle of the missing lady, and, although he cannot give us any clue to her possible whereabouts, yet he has joined actively in the search for her, and has rendered us some valuable aid. This morning Desmond's advertisement appeared in the first column of the Times, asking for information of Beryl Star. It was by that name she was known in Bayswater. No answer has yet appeared to the advertisement, but it is too soon to look for it. It is very singular how near we have repeatedly come to finding her. Desmond saw her in Wells. street. Mrs. Margie encountered her in Picca- dilly, and yesterday she was in the Bayswater house when we called there, and we saw her leave the house in disguise." "It is singular," said the earl. "Oh! if you had only intercepted her." Beryl was in a far corner of the room, in a chair turned away from the group round the earl. She could hear all, herself unseen. Sie was very silent now, but her heart fluttered wildly. " We were all together in Desmond's chambers when my clerk came around with your message, my Lord," said Sherwald, with a growing and apparent nervousness. "The clerk had waited for my return until he had despaired of my coming, instead of seeking me out promptly. I read your letter and gave it into Desmond's hands. The result of the discovery he made was to hurry us all here together. And now, my Lord, may we ask who penned that letter ? ' "My attendant, a gentlewoman, who has waited upon me since yesterday morning, and who has saved my life," declared the earl, emphati- cally. "These vipers you see here, and who remain when I told them to leave my house, have begun upon me a regular system of poisoning. Nothing else whatever has been the matter with me from the first. This develish woman, Octavia, prepared the stuff for me to drink, and I drank it unsuspectingly. I should have been stark and stiff in death at this moment if Mrs. Park had not detected the infamous design and completely out- witted Mrs. Conyers." "Who is Mrs. Park?' asked Sherwald. "Who recommended her to you, my Lord ?" "My housekeeper, Mrs. Dominick." "How does Mrs. Park look ?" asked Desmond, eagerly • "Does she dress in black?' "Yes, and wear spectacles and a widow's cap." "Will you summon her, Lord Hawkhurst ?" asked Desmond, arising, flushed an eager. "Certainly. She's in the room now. Mrs. Park."

Beryl trembled and looked about for some avenue of flight. There was none. She could not own up to her imposition and a wild idea came to her of braving out the ordeal that had come upon her. The earl called her more loudly. She arose and came forward, the picture of an elderly, frightened, subdued little gentlewoman, her false hair banded smoothly away from her spectacles. "This is Mrs. Park, the lady to whom I owe my life," said the earl "Mrs. Park, let me introduce to you Mr. Desmond, my kinsman; Mr. Sherwald, my solicitor, and Mr. Star. Now, gentleman, what have you to say of Mrs. Park ?" Sherwald looked at his companions. "I have nothing to say, except to apologize for troubling her," said Mr. Star. " We—l had a fancy that she might be my niece, after all. Mr. Desmond thought he recognised the handwriting as Beryl's. I see that this lad3r cannot be Beryl, and our latest hope is destroyed." Mr. Sherwald's countenance expressed his disap- pointment. But noble Desmond stepped forward, radiant and joyful "Beryl I" he said softly. "Oh, Beryl, I have found you at last I" To the profound astonishment of all the spec- tators the elderly little gentlewoman gave a sharp cry. of anguish and retreated before him.

Did -you think -iciti-w;uTraiszi; yourself beyond my recognition, Beryl ?'' Aced Desmond, tenderly. "No ; you shall not escape from mo. I have got you at last." He caught her in his arms. She struggled to free herself, and succeeded.
- " You have found me out, Noble," she said, her tones full of keen pain. "It would have been better to let me alone. This disguise is useless now. and_l will not retain it."

She took off her widow's cap, wig, spectacles, and wet her handkerchief from the carafe of water upon the table and washed the stain off her face. She stood revealed as Beryl Star, in all her youth, innocence and glorious beauty—Beryl with the sombre eyes so dusky stars. The earl stared at her speechlessly. "Beryl," said Mr. Star, "I ask you to forgive all my cruelty to you. When I heard that you were missing, I feared that I had been the cause of your death. I offer you a home at Starwood, and if you will come to me I will make you my heir." " Beryl," said Desmond, eagerly, "oh, come to me! Forget that illusion regarding the existence of your first husband and be my own cherished wife. Beryl, my wife—" "Wait, Noble 1" said Beryl, with a sorrowful smile. "Let me answer Mr. Star first. I thank you, sir, for your kindness, but I can never go to Starwood as one on sufferance." "But, Beryl, you were not to blame," said Mr. Star. "1 have usurped the privileges of the Almightly and visited the sins of the parents on the head of their innocent offspring. I will make amends for my wicked brutality. I will give yot. my name, adopt you legally, and—" "Stay !" said the earl. "Is this girl Bery Slur

"Yes," said Mr. Star and Desmond, in a breath. "The daughter of Jenny Star ?" Mr. Star uttered a hesitating affirmative. "Then she has no need of being adopted by any, one," said the earl, standing erect. " Thia girl Is my daughter, and as snch I acknowledge her Iln the presence of you all!" There was a general exclamation of incredulity. Lord Hawkhurst held out his arms to Beryl, but she shook her head sorrowfully and would not approach him. And yet she felt the subtle magnetism of his presence and could have flown to him' but for the memory of her mother's fate. "You have the Hawkhurst pride, I see, Beryl," said the earl. "I know what you have been taught regarding your origin, and I now declare to you that Jenny Star was my lawful wife, and that you are legally and truly my daughter and only child, Lady Beryl Desmond I' His lordship's words carried conviction with them. The group around stood speechless. "An explanation is due you, my daughter, and you, also, Mr. Star," said the earl, resuming his test through sudden weakness. I became acquaintsd with Jenny Star when she was governess and companion in the family of Lady Fortescue. Miss Star was called in to play the piano very often, and, indeed, spent most of her evenings in the drawing-room. Notwithstanding her position and lack of birth, she had several admirers above her own rank of life. I had come into my title, was a widower and childless. My first marriage had been one of convenience. I loved Jenny Star with all the ardour of my fierce nature. She loved me. I asked her to marry me and she con-iented. My mother was living then— a haughty, iligh-bred lady, who was building great hopes upon second marriage she was planning for me. Jei..ty was not versed in society ways, and I formed the idea of moulding her to my wishes. I m,,rried her secretly, and established a home for her at St. John's Wood. We lived there together a year in perfect happi- ness. Then Jenny began to importune me to acknowledge our marriage. Between her and my mother, who was anxious that I should marry a lady she had chosen for me, I grew impatient and ill-tempered. I began to stay away from our villa for days together, not that I loved Jenny less, but that I did not like to be so constantly importuned. We had a terrible quarrel one day— Jenny and I —and I left her, declaring to her that I would never acknowledge her. They were words spoken in the heat of passion, and God knows I did not mean them. My poor Jenny! My lost wife! Have I not been terribly punished for those wild, angry words since ?" He wiped his face, which was working with agi- tation and wet with a cold sweat. 'I had scarcely left her, when my mother, who had in some way discovered my villa at St. John's Wood, arrived, and had an interview with my wife. My mother assured her that I had repented my folly in taking Jenny to myself, and that I loved a noble lady and desired to marry her. My mother confessed this and much more to me on her death-bed, a year later. I went home late that night, remorseful, and resolved to acknow- ledge my wife immediately. I went, I say, but I found her gone. Gone, and leaving no trace! Gone, my wife, my loved one! How madly I searched for her I Weeks later I sent a confiden- tial letter to Starwood, to learn if she had gone ' back to her kindred. He brought me word that she was dead and told me where she was buried. I visited her grave. I would have taken up her body and interred it among those of my own people, but my mother dissuaded me, and it could ' have done no good. I never knew until very recently that she—my wife—had borne a child. I do not deserve your love, Beryl; I dare not ask it; yet I see your mother's eyes in yours, and if you were only to forgive me the cruel wrong I dl her, I think that my wife in heaven would smile Upon us and ratify that forgiveness." He turned a pleading gaze upon his child. And Beryl, with a choking sob, flew to his arms. A little later, Lord Hawk aurst said, unsteadily: "And so, Beryl, you are Desmond's wife? He is a noble fellow. Dismiss your illusions, and put your hand in his like a loving wife. Desmond Beryl drew back from her father's embrace, her brightness overshadowed. "It was no illusion about my first husband," she said. "Papa—Noble—have you not guessed the truth? There stands the man I married in Geneva last August—the man I married as Dane Conyers—the man who had so nearly wrecked my life And he is my husband still." Conyers smiled after a ghastly fashion. "Yes," he said, "I am her husband." "He?" cried the earl. "It is Conyers ! But it will be easy to procure a divorce. We will see to it at once.' "But what is Oetavia, if the Lady Beryl is Conyers 's wife ?" asked Callender. "She has lost Cragthorpe, lost husband—everything." "It's all up !" said Conyers, crossing the floor with a graceful step and laughing mirthlessly. "The divorce will be easy to procure, as Lord Hawkhurst says. Oetavia has lost her fortune. I am likely to be arrested for bigamy. It's a bad ending for a life that began as fair as mine." He went to the cabinet and took out the goblet , witn the poisoned draught. ! "I drink to your healths, all of you," he cried. "My Lady Beryl, permit me to wish you happi• ness in your second marriage. I was not all bail; I have loved you from urst to last; I love you still." And he lifted the poisoned goblet to his lip and drank the draught that had been intendea for the earl. His movement had been too quick for those wile would have intercepted him. He dropped the glass and fell to the floor—dead! The fragrancE of bitter almonds on his lips told what agent had been employed to dissolve the tie that unites thE soul to the body. They buried him among his kindred. Mr. Cal. lender took his niece away from England, and she resumed her maiden name, and lived a life thence- forward whose bitterness only those who have beer guilty like her, and baulked in all their ambitions, can understand. Loathing her life, yet afraid tc die—could her worst enemy have wished her E worse fate? Lord Hawkhurst publicly acknowledged hi: marriage to Jenny Star, and acknowledged also the Lady Beryl Desmond as his daughter and heiress The remains of ill-fated Jenny were taken up fron their untionoured resting-place and reinterred b 3 the side of the proud Lady Hawkhurst who hac caused her death. Mr. Windsor of Cragthorpe took possession of his own, married, and lived happily in the home which Conyers had schemed to win. Of all ths characters whom we have depicted ir our true narrative, not one was happier in the acknowledgment of Beryl as the earl's daughtee than Mr. Star. His sister's name was cleared All his grimness disappeared, and the old boyish geniality that had once characterized him bloomed forth anew. His house was opened to his friends and in time he contracted a desirable marriage and was greatly blessed. For many years he hai not spoken his sister's name, but now a doze: times each day he finds occasion to mention "m: Sister' the late Lady Hawkhurst," or "my niece the Lady Beryl Desmond." THE END.

On an all-round computation the mortality rates of the British Isles compare very favourably indeed with those of other countries. We have made a profound study of hygiene, sanitation, etc. Mereover, the young idea is instinctively imbued with the value to health of bodily exercise and health-giving recreation. The pr f - valent vices of continental schools, to take an example, are all but unknown in this country. We live a saner and healthier life altogether. Yet it must not he thought that every physicist condition is in our favour. Our climate is cold and treacherous, and certainly our gen- eral dietary is open to improvement. Both these con- ditions militate against us to some extent, and medicinal cot rectives are more needed here than any. here else. The heating food (which is to some extent necessary in a climate like ours) brings about a sluggishness of tie liver, a lethargic state of the whole alimentary system which has to he fought against constantly. Fortu- nately the means are at hand, and California Syrup of Figs stands in the forefront as a really efficient laxative, and quite alone as a pleasant and altogether agreeable medicine. div.head: SATURDAY POPULAR CONCERTS 1N PARR HALL.
div.p: THE SATURDAY POPULAR CONCERTS 1N PARR HALL.

The audience at the Parr Hall, on Saturday even- ing,was one of the largest which has yet been seen at the Saturday evening popular concerts, and an- other satisfactory feature was the excellent pro- gramme provided. The chief attraction was, of course, the appearance of the Merrions- who de- lighted the audience with their entertainment. On them fell the greater portion of the work of enter- taining, and it must be admitted that they dis- charged their duties with success, and to the satis- faction of all present. The opening item was a humorous trio " The mixed Vocalists" by the Merrions.. Individual items were after- wards given by Mr. Will Merrion, who gave an original humorous sketch entitled "On and off a bicycle." and Mr. Fred Merrion,who contributed an eccentric sketch entitled "I todole along with the Mail Cart." Both sketches were cleverly given,and the audience showed their appreciation by con- tinued applause. A musical melange, in which a variety on instruments was introduced,and very suc- cessfully performed upon by Messrs.W.and H.Mer- rion,was the concluding item of the first half of the programme. The audience was kept in a continual state of mirth during the performance of the humorous trio " The Bungleton Town Councillors," and the amusing'farce " April fools," both of which have been arranged by W. Merrion. But perhaps the most novel feature of the entertainment was the " Living Pictures from the Music Sellers," by Mr. H. Merrion, in which pictures were used to illustrate the characters in several of the popular songs of the day. It is a matter of course to say that the Merrions were heartily received, and their performances much enjoyed. They were accom- ponied on the piano by Mr. J. E. Warhurst. The vocalists engaged were, Miss Rose Bushell (soprano). Mies Juanita Jones (contralto), and Mr. Arthur Weber (bass ) Miss Jones gave an excellent interpretation of " The Heavenly Song," and in responding to the continued applause of the audience she complied with Daddy," which still further pleased her hearers. She was also encored for he: fine rendering of "Through Sunny Spain." Miss Bushell did not do herself justice in her first song, but was far more successful in her interpretation of " The Carnival." Mr. Arthur Weber has gained a high reputation with Warrington audiences, and on Saturday he more than maintained it. "The Star of the Desert" and "Behold, I stand at the door" were both well suited to his voice, and they were sung with a depth of f.,eling and impressiveness. Replying to the recalls he sang "The Boys of the Old Brigade" and "Rocked in the Cradle of the Deep." Mr. Thomas Lane accompanied the vocalists.

div.head: BOYCOTTING OF CO-OPERATORS
div.p: THE BOYCOTTING OF CO-OPERATORS
IN SCOTLAND.

The butchers' boycott movement has collapsed in Edinburgh. At a special meeting of the master butchers held on Monday night it was unanimously agreed to die. solve the Trade Defence Association, and that body at a subsequent meeting put the resolution into effect. The " Scotsman " states that in Glasgow too the tables have been turned upon the boycotters at Yorkhill. The ex- pulsion, or defection, of Mr. T. C. Nelson, one of the ' most influential salesmen of the cattle of American con- signers, was a week aeo treated with scorn by leaders of the movement in Glasgow. At Monday's sales the boy- cotters found that their supplies were not forward. Mr. Nelson had secured the support of the American con- signers for the open market system. An attempt on the part of the boycotters to arrange for supplies from Bir- kenhead was frustrated. There will probably be an effort to protract the struggle, but the example of the Edinburgh butchers in washing their hands of the whole affair will not be without its effect, and the end of the boycott is not now far off.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW POLICE BUILDINGS.
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW POLICE BUILDINGS.

The question of a site for Oka new police buildings for Warrington was fur- ther discussed at a meeting of the Watch Committee last weak. It was ultimately agreed to submit two sites for the consideration of the Council at their meeting in March, viz.: the Barracks site And a second site near the Town Hall. The latter iS not the same as was recommended to the Council a month ago. It, is proposed to extend the Town Hall buildings across the intervening space leading to Bath-st., and to remove the Volun- teer buildings near the Drill Hall, This is really carrying out a suggestion made by Mr. R. T. Faircleugh some years ago. It is believed that there will be ample room to meet the requirements of the police, without encroaching on the Park at all. It would of course be necessary to close the Bath-street entrance to the Park,but it is soggested that another could be provided at the other Bide of the Town Hall near the recreation ground. In or- der to continue the means or communication be- tween Sankey-street and Bath-street an archway would be provided in the new buildings. This scheme met with considerable favour by many members of the Watch Committee,and the Borough Surveyor is now engaged in preparing further in- formation on the subject.

MY DEAR NELLIE. A pretty toque which will brighten up the quietest dress and make an old one look ultra smart, is of the turban shape in the new fluffy material that the milliners call horsehair gauze. The colour is creamy white, and it has no trimming save the half bandeau of turquoise velvet bows, Which raises it on the left side, and the group of two black and two white ostriah tips also on the left, held in place with a turquoise and paste orna- ment.

—ce possessor of two ostrich tips of rather un- usual height should apply them to a toque of felt, cloth, or velvet. One tip should stand up erect on the left, where the toque is bunched up, and the feather should curl over from loft to right. The other tip should be laid flat on the left, so as to curl over the hair at the back. Its stalk, which starts from the same root as the other tip, should be disguised by a loop of velvet or ribbon drawn through a buckle.

A very pretty dress for a young girl is made in pale blue veiling with ivory lace and a blue sash, or is charming in white or cream,with blue or pink ribbon round the waist. Both of these dresses fasten at the back, but the opening is kept as im- perceptible as possible. The little yoke may be of pale-coloured silk in a white dress, or of thin white silk in a coloured one. Both sleeves and bodice are arranged on fitted linings, and the skirt, and bodice connected by a narrow band.

The closely-cut shirt has a facing of velvet, laid flab, and cut to shape, the sides rising to one-third of the depth, and outlined with a narrow border of astraclaan. The short coat has a wide collar of velvet, divided on the shoulders in rever fashion, and the vest and cuffs are also of velvet. ,gAlthough the newest silk skirts set closely at the de,, there is pienty of fulness at the back, but irs is arrangod more by gores and sloping seams 4.t'an by actual width, as few skirts measure more "u an four-and-a-quarter yards, while four yards is a very general measurement. WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

' A meeting of this Council was held in the Coun- cil Chamber at the Town Hall,on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Wright) presided, and there were also president Aldermen Fairclough, Black- hurst, Sutton, Hutchinson, Francomb, Councillors H. Poberts, F. R. Roberts, John Roberts, J. Shaw Green, G. Plumpton, Smethurst, Bennett, Evans, Ellison, Duncan, Tinnion, Peacocke, Furness,Rogers, Woods, Shillcock, Wilkinson, Heaton, Lee., Bennett, Grace, Crosfield, Jolley, Longton, with Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Mr. Stanley Wilson (deputy town clerk), Mr. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Mr. Longdin (borough surveyor), Mr. Dees (sanitary engineer), Mr. S. Haddock (gas engineer.) THE LETTING OF OLD WARPS.—A HEATED DISCUSSION. The Finance and Estate Committee made the follow- ing recommendations :—That the premises at Market Gate. recently occupied by Mr. John Hatton, be let to Boots, Cash Chemists (W(stern) Limited, at the rent of £133 per annum ; that the farm at the Old Warps be let to Mr. E. Bennett, at the rent of £5O per annum,suhject to the terms of an agreement to be prepared by the Town Clerk; that the Old Warps residence be let to Mrs. Davies on a monthly tenancy,at a rent after the rate of £5O per annum ; and that the land in Howley, adjoining the Store Yard, be let to Mr. Patrick Moffatt en aequarterly tenancy, at a rent after the rate of £l5 per annum. Councillor Srtew GREEN moved the confirmation of the minutes and said that the shop at Market-gate was not let on a yearly tenancy, but so that they could get pos- se3sion at any time within a reasonable period. With regard to Old Warpa,the committee had been endeavour- ing to deal with the property so as to bring back a con- siderable proportion of the cost. He had asked for plans to be laid before the Council. .
_ Councillor WOODS objected to these plans as they had only been laid before the committee the previous after- noon. _ . .

The MAYOR: CouncillerShaw Green simply wishes to explain. Councillor &Kew GREEN said that after the Street Im- provement Committee had widened the road to sixty feet the full length of the estate, they then proposed to deal with the corner,now a willow-bed. They would let off two strips of land for building purposes one of which would front the highway and the other the proposed park. Councillor Wows again objected to going on with that as it had only come before the committee on the previous day. The MAYOR thought it would perhaps be better to confine attention to what they were letting, leaving out what they propoq3d to do hereafter. Councillor SHAW GREEN eaid they proposed to let the agricultural land—the farm at the top end, together with the farmhouse,to Mr. Bennett for fi() for the year. They also proposed to let the house to Mrs. Davies. The land to he actually let was 22 acres but there was also the privilege of grazing the land that was to be used for park purposes. They had advertised the .place to let but they had had only one application, and it was from Mr. Bennett who offered -22 an acre or £44. Several members of the committee suggested .that they might get more money for it if they waited for other people to bid and it was intimated to the proposed ten- ant that very probably the committee would accept £5O. He then raised his offer to £5O and though they had re- ceived another offer of £5O they deemed it advisable to accept the original offer. The DEPUTY MAYOR seconded the adoption of the minutes. _

Councillor Szaarnmast asked if Mr. Singleton, the other gentleman who had made an offer, had not in- creased his offer of £5O to £52 (" No non Councillor ErnsoN wanted to know when it was pro- posed to open a portion of the Park to the public. He. thought it was important that soraevertion of it should' be opened this summer. (Hear, bear.) Councillor LEE said that although a member of the committee he felt obliged to move an amendment that the portion of the minutes referring to the letting of the land at OA Warps to Mr. Bennett be referred back His reason was that they were getting nothing like an equivalent to the value of the farm. The piece of land at Howley they were letting to Mr. Patrick Moffatt was five statute acre, with no building upon it and they were getting £3 a statute acre, yet they were proposing to let 22 acres of farm land with buildings and the right of grazing over 30 acres for the nominal suili of £5O. It was to his- mind the most unbusinesslike and unsatisfactory trans- action he ever came across, considering that the same area was formerly let for £l3O a year. Take the graz- ing land of 30 acres alone. It it carried 100 sheep at 3d. per week per head the tenant would get mere than his rent from it immediately. That estate cost the Corpora- tion £10;000 but there was no reasonable 'probability that they would ever recover a tenth part of the money. Councillor H. ROBERTS : Nonsense; you will let your building land at what will cover the whole of the inter- est of the money. (Hear, hear.) Councillor LEE said he differed from that statement. Councillor &mom seconded the amendment. The Durant MAYOR thought Councillor Lee had not stated eveything that occurred at the Finance Com- mittee meeting. Councillor Les; I should be very sorry to do so. (Laughter.) The DEPUTY MAYOR said there were two applicants at the finish, one Mr. Singleton and the other Mr. Bennett, and Councillor Lee actually proposed that Singleton should have the place at £5O a year, but this proposal was lost. Therefore, if Councillor Lee bad had his way the farm would have been let at the same rent. . .

'Councillor Lin] said he ought to explain that one of his objections was that the second application of Mr. Bennett was a verbal one. It was not conveyed to the committee in writing at all. If Mr. Singleton had had the samo chance he would have offered £6O a year or more. Councillor WOODS said he did like fair play in a ques- tion of that kind. The increased offer placed before the Committee was a ver:Jal one. Bath the tenders were produced by the Chairman and they were open though they ought to be opened in the presence of the Commit- tee. (Hear, hear.) They had paid £lO,OOO for the estate and the interest upon it was £350, so that if they only got £lOO back again there would be a loss of £250. He thought they ought to get as much as they possibly could to reduce the rates. He understood that the Bret applicant was told by an official of the Corporation that if he offered £5O he would get the land. Mr. FAIII.HURST (borough treasurer) : That is not so. Councillor %You's said if they gave one man two
L
_ genuine nn Noble only be obta,

div.head: EST
div.p: EST

chances why not give the other man the same ? What they were paying in interest on bought property Was equal to a penny in the Z. Councillor GRACE said the sidelights they had had up- on the proceedings of the Finance Committee, were not of an edifying description. fle supported the amend- ment. Councillor Fl, ROBERTS wished to get at the actual facts of the case. The Committee, he understood, only received one tender as a reply to their advertisement and that tender was for something less than £5O. At a second Finance Committee meeting held a fortnight later than when the original tender was received two , tenders were put before the Committee. One of these was the advanced offer of the person who originally tendered. A MEMBER: A verbal offer. '

Councillor H. ROBERTS Was it communicated to the Committee through the borough treasurer that the man who made the first offer had verb illy increased the offer to £5O ("Yes"). Well, he might be a little bit obtuse but he wanted to he clear. This verbal offer increasing the original offer from the only man who tendered was put before the Finance Committee through the medium of the borough treasurer, and at the same tims another offer was received from another gentleman of the same amount. Then the Committee had to decide between these two. What were they to think of the deep finan- sial interes Cotylcillor bee took in that question when he was so desirous that this matter should be referred back simply on the ground, as he protested, that they were not getting as much for the land as they ought to get ? Yet Councillor Lee himself was the man to pro- pose that the second tender should be accepted. What value where they to attach to the protests of a member of that Council that they were not getting all they should get when as a matter of fact he himself was pre- pared to let the place at £5O to a tenant who happened to suit his purpose ? (Hear, hear.) It was a question of the men and not the price at all. Councillor Lae : I have not the sliahtest interest in either of them, and Councillor Ro'serts has no right to make these insinuations.

Councillor H, Roncirrs said be had a perfect right to make deductions from the action of a gentleman which was not consistent with the action of a few days ago. Councillor LEE : You have not ascertained all the facts, Councillor H. ROBERTS said he had ascertained quito sufficient of the facts to answer his nurpose. Councillor Lee must either believe that the offer was good enough or that it WRS not good enough. am:minor LEE : I do not believe it was good enough. Councillor ROBERTS said it had not been a question of the amount to be received from the farm. The only error the Committee had made was in not accepting Singleton instead of Bennett. Councillor BENNETT thought they ought to get more than £5O a year for that property, but he wished to know why they were letting it at all, seeing that it was to be applied to the purposes of a park and recreation ground. The Mayon said the pertion dedicated to the public was Rot being let at all except for grazing purposes. Councillor BENNETT said that no specific portion was definitely dedicated to the publ:c, but he thought that it was important that it should be.

Councillor Tinmon thought there had been an irregu- larity on the part of some menalaer or members of the committee. When they were dealing with tenders all the conditions of the tender should be fulfilled. His reason for supporting the amendment was that they had net got the best possible price for that land, and another was that everything should be done in a straightforward way that was above suspicion of any kind. This Old Warps estate was a growing white ele- phant. ("No, no.") Alderman ns/semis said he had been told hy 74dr. Singleton that he was prepared to give £7O a year for that land. He would be prepared to give a bigger price than £5O himself. He suggested that the minutes should be withdrawn.

Councillor LONGTOW supported the amendment. He dissented from the statement that the Old Warps would •be a white elephant. The DEPUTY MAYOR • How can you withdraw it when you told the man he could have the land? The TOWN CLERIC He is in possession. In answer to Councillor FURNESS it was stated that tenders were invited by advertisement. Councillor Sgew GREEN said he had been astonished by the course of that discussion. There had been no ir- regularity,no side-lights, and nothing beneath the sur- face. Al that had been done had been done ?.learly and straightforwardly. The first tender was one dated 19th September and was the only one in response to an advertisement that appeared four •consecutive weeks ia the whole of the three papers In Warrington. They did everything they could to bring the matter under the notice of the Inhabitants of the district and they had one tender. That tender was for £44. Two or three members of the committee thought they might get more and did their best to get more. The gentleman who had tendered was one day in the office of the borough treasurer and the borough trea- surer suggested to him that he should give £5O. The second tender was not opened by us. The Tows Cu= : I opened it. Councillor Saaw-Gaegg said it was brotrht down to the committe and it was for £5O. They then had two applications before thetn. They were both for £5O. and the question therefore was one not of money but of men. Three•members of the committee supported Mr. Bennett and two Mr. Singleton, and they had therefore accepted Mr. Bennett. What had they liner to take back? The amendment WAS then put to the vote and as 20 members voted for the amendment and only six against, the amendment that the minute referring to the letting of the farm at Old WArps be referre4 back was carried.

div.head: lEttirld COMMITTEIL—FORCHABE OF PROPERTY.
div.p: lEttirld COMMITTEIL—FORCHABE OF PROPERTY.

At a meeting of this committee it was resolved that the Town Clerk be authorised to offer to Mr. William Wheeler the sum of £545 for the purchase of the free- hold ef the premises .belonging to him in Angel-yard and Hill street, Town-hill. Alderman !SUTTON, in [reeving the confirmation of the minutes, said he believed She offer made to Mi. Wheeler would be accepted,and in the agreement he undertook te redeem the ground rent at a cost of £240, in order to make the property freehold. The committee considered it was desirable,in the interests of the town, that the property should he purchased. The minutes were secnded iv Councillor H.RcEitaTS and confirmed. TELE PAVING 0F STREETS NEAR CHURCHES.
--- At a meeting of the Paving and Sewerage Committee a letter was read from the trustees of St. Mary's Mission
X AMMER, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 4, 1898.

.atchford (with a plan showing the site of a proposed new church in St. Mary's-street),requesting the Corpora- tion to forego the charge for street making on an under- taking being given that the church should be built, fail- ing which the money should be paid, when it was resolved that the request be acceded to on condition that the trustees pay interest at the rate of four per cent, on the amount of the apportionment in respect of the pro- posed church until such church be built, and if the erection of the Church be not commenced within three years, then the trustees must apply to the Finance Com- mittee for a farther extension of time.

The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the minutes, and said the committee had a great amount of work in hand, and they hoped to make considerable progress during the coming year if they could get material for it. Councillor ElsaTox seconded. Councillor ELLisoN said he had been requested to bring before the Council the desirability of paving St. , Mary's-street and more especially opposite the proposed church to be erected there, with wood blocks. The MAYOR said this question had beets carefully con. sidered by the committee, and they would meet the applicants with the same fair spirit as they had met other denominations. Councillor H. ROBERTS While you are paving round all the churches would you consider the desirability of paving round Wycliffe Church ? (Laughter.) There is macadam paving at the front, and setts at the side, which disturbs our devotions considerably when any traffic passes by. If the committee is going to treat some of the denominations in this kind spirit it ought to be extended to the older denominations in our midst. (Hear, hear.)

Councillor'SniETacasi. : We shall be very pleased to have the streets around St. Paul's Church paved with wood. (Laughter.) Councillor Claacz : Pave also in front of the council- lors' houses with wood. (Laughter.) The MAYOR I think I can promise you that the com- mittee will take the matter into consideration. The minutes were then confirmed. THE STANDARD OF EXEMPTION FOR SCHOOL

when Mr. Cooper was at the office. This year there would be gathered over £3,000 in coppers alone. With regard to Mr. Smith, the committee were only asking the Council to give the wages Mr. Howard received be- fore he was appointed to Mr. Cooper's place. Councillor HEATON seconded the motion, and asked the Council to consider the fact that the Gas Depart- ment was one which made a profit. They should well consider their servants who had been with them a long time. Councillor Sitirriciasx asked the committee to take into their serious consideration the question of the re- duction in the price of gas which was now being paid in Warrington. The Mews : That is hardly befote us to-night,Coun- cillor Smethurst. . .

-6C-11.1717610-r-gld-ETHI7II.9T : You seem to be very anxious to raise salaries, whatever becomes of the consumers of gas. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Girece supported the minutes of the com- mittee, remarking that he believed the officials in ques- tion had well earned the proposed increases. Re should I like to say that now the dark nights were leaving them and there would not be the same consumption-- of gas, some steps ought to be taken to improve the pressure of the gas. Re was perfectly satisfied that the gas was good, but the great fault was shortness of pressure. The minutes were then agreed to.

-- THE SHIP CANAL, COMPANY'S CHARGE!. The Water Committee at a meeting held on January 24th resolved that an acknowledgment of £2 2s. per an- num be paid to the Manchester Ship Canal Company for permission to construct a 6-inch iron pipe Over the Bridgewater Canal and adjoining lands of the coin-

pany. Alderman Falacoons proposed the passing of the minutes. Councillor Ls seconded, and said the acknowledg- ment it was proposed to pay to the Ship Canal Company was another instance of the manner in which that com- pany were treating Warrington. A sum of 10s.or 25.61. would have been ample to pay. (Hear, hear.) The minutes ware agreed to. ALDERMAN SUTTON AND THE WIDENING OF BRIDGE-STREET. THE PRICES OF PROPERTY.

At the General Purposes Committee meeting held on January 24th the draft of an Order of the Local Govern- ment Board conferring on the Council certain powers of a Parish Council under the Lecal Government Act, 1894, was submitted by the Town Clerk, and ordered to be printed. It was resolved that in the interests of trade, industry, and social convenience it is essential that the fullest possible development of the telephone service in this country should be promoted ; that in order to effect such development it is necessary that only a moderate rental be charged • that the best and cheapest service can only be secured by competition. That as the Trea- sury Minute, dated 23rd May, 1892, provides, as a matter of general policy, " that competition shall not be , prevented," this Council earnestly requests the Post- master General to grant licenses without injury as to the charges or efficiency of the present service to any 'municipalities or companies which comply with the requirements of the Treasury Minute, such inquiries being inconsistent with the spirit of the Treasury Minute end involving unnecessary expense and delay ; that this Council desires particularly to support the claim for licenses made by the new Mutual Telephone Company, Limited, of Manchester, and by the Corporation of Glas- gow. The Town Clerk reported the result of the inter- view with the Main Roads and Bridges Committee of the Lancashire Co.inty Council on the subject of the I proposed new bridge, but as the copy resolution which the committee promised to send had net yet been received the consideration of the matter was deferred. It was also resolved that the common seal of the Borough be affixed to the following documents :—Two references to arbitration ; agreement with Boot's, Cash Chemists (Western) Limited ; agreement with Freeman, Hardy, and Willis, Limited ; agreement with R. I. Blackburne for the purchase of land off Winwick-road. The MAYOE moved, and the DEPUTY MAYOR seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Alderman SUTTON asked for an explanation of an item in the minutes which read :—'• Orders were made for the payments of accounts amounting to £345 13s, 4d." Had it reference to the widening of Bridge-street ? The MAYOR : I am sorry to say that without notice I cannot answer the question. Alderman SUTTON : Without notice ! Does anyane know? The MkTOR : I think we can get the information. The DEPUTY Mayon: There is nothing in the accounts about the widening of Bridge-street. Alderman Surrom : Are we to pass the account with- out someone being able to tell us what it is for The Maros : I don't say that, be. I do say that one ought to have had reasonable notice of the question. Can you give the information,Mr.Treasurer? I cannot carry all these things in my mind. Alderman SUTTON: Surely someone ought to be able Ito answer an open question of this sort—s)rne member of the committee, at any rate. 1 The Mato& : lam sorryl cannot. I should have to have a very extensive memory to carry all these things in my bead. I think you ought to have given us rea- sonable notice.
Alderman SUTTON : How could I when it only ap- pears on the agenda paper ? The dls.roa : I tell you candidly at once that I can* not answer the question.. . . .

Councillor GRACE : The information can to obtained in two or three minutes. The MAYOR: I have no deabt it can, but in a case like this reasonable notice ought to have been given, The TONWN CLERIC : If it is the dlderman'a desire to discuss the volition of the widening of Bridge-street he can do so on the last motion of the Committee's minutes. Alderman SUTTON I want to know what is being done. The Mayors : The minutes refer to the arbitration of the Bridge-street property. Alderman SUTTON : It appears to me that there is scarcely a member of the Council who understands any- thing about the matter. Continuing, he said he wished to ask how it was that the sub-committees appointed years ago had never condescended to make a report as to the negotiations which had gone on from tim3 to time up to the present, and why they had detertnineu to , keep the General Pusposes Committee and the Council I in the dark, and in the uncliguitied position when asked for information that they had to reply that they knew nothing at all about the matter? NJ reason.was given for tlae delay in th 3 widening of the street. He emphasized the term " undignified," be- cause it was most undignified and humiliating for any member of thc Council to be in such a position and to be obliged to confess his ignorance. It had been agreed by at least one member of the Council that there had been no necessity to furnish a report, inasmuch as the com- mittee appointed were delegates with full power and authority to negotiate and purchase. But the General Purposes Committee ought to be told what had ben done in the matter, so that something could be known. Properties were censtantly purchased in various parts of the town for all sorts of purposes at a very large ex- pense. In one case particularly a purchase was made of property before either the committee concerned or the Council knew anything abut the matter. (A voice: " Which ?'') The particular properties in Bridge-street had been in the meantime utterly overlooked and neg. The Mayon: I am advised ',au are out of order. lteioctnedoitomtahneysurprise of everybody and to the indigna e Have you anything to object to in the resolution at the bottom of the page. The matter is now in a way to being brought to a close. Alderman SUTTON : We have been told that for years back. The MAYOR : I am obliged to stop you. he minutes, in Alderman SUTTON : Nothing has appeared on the minutes. It seems to have been the motive and inten- otirodnero ft that we n mat- ters. I once gave a notice of motion that I would bring the matter under the notice of the Council, ee aet ity o not keep everything ee vaeuriay tthoindgi off the certain t bat I was induced not to do so--I was induced to withdraw it. The MAYOR : Let us keep to the minutes. You know the rules as well as anyone. Have you anythiug to say as to the resolution with reference to the agreements relating to streets ? Alderman SUTTON : I say it is an Injustice to per- chess land while Bridge-st. is neglected. It is becoming a public scandal. I say it is not right ; it is not fair either to landlord or tenant, because of the difficulty they are in. They don't kla ow what to do. Tenants are in a state of great anxiety because their living is en- tirely dependent noon the matter. It is time that some- thing was done.. The newspapers bad been very much misled in the matter, when they Stated net exorbitant prices had been asked for the property. Councillor H. ROBERTS : People have been aelling ex- orbitant prices. Alderman SUTTON : It has'sot beEdi so in all <1 Less. Councillor H. ROBERTS : In all Cases of prcperty not purchased. Councillor WOODS : Is the matter on the minutes ? The Mayor ought to rule the discussion out of order. Alderman Surrom : I pay due deference to you. Mr. Mayor. (Cries of "Chair,chair.") It was a gross mis- representation of facts to put forward what was stated

in the newspapers, that the owners, one and all, had been demanding exorbitant prices from the ratepayers. Councillor WOODS : I object to this Council heicig made into a public advertising medium for a gentleman connected with any particular department of business. Ibis taking up our time unnecessarily. Alderman SuTroN : It will not be at the instigation of Councillor Woods, who jumps up like a.' jack-in-the box." (Cries of " Chair," " chair,"" chair.") I will pay respect to the Mayor. Councillor WOODS : You have not done so, or you would have sat down.

The Mayon here rang his bell for the purpose of call- ing the members to order. Councillor H. ROBERTS rose to speak. Alderman Surrom : I shall object to Councillor Roberta speaking if I am refused. (" Chair," " chair.")

The School Attendance Committee recommended the acceptance of the following resolution :—" That, in the opinion of this committee, the standard for total exemp- tion from attendance be raised to the sixth standard provided that the Privy Council sanction a bylaw per- mitting the employment of children who have reached the fifth standard in any case in which the conamittee may be satisfied that such child may be beneficially and necessarily employed." Councillor SHAW GREEN, in moving the confirmation of the minutes,said the above resolution had been passed owing to a great number of children of very young age running about the streets having passed the fifth stan- dard by special examination, and who were unable to get employment, and who were losing all the benefit of their attendance at school. In 1896 out of 665 children who passed the labour examination 534 were wandering about the streets until they had an oppartunity of going to work opened out to them. In the past year 607 were examined, and 521 were not able to find employment. CouncillorSinucock seconded the confirmation of the minutes. The MAYOR I considet it a very wise resolution, and I am surprised Tau did not arrive at it years ago provid- ing you can get the Government'a sanction. The minutes were then confirmbd. A COMPLIMENT TO THE WARRINGTON MUSEUM. THE PROPOSED ART EXHIBITION.

e° moving the confirmation of the minutes incuitea onithrl MEußsresu'm ill ,Library,Arts,and Technical Instruction Committee, said he should like to mention incidentally a matter of much interest -ehich was re- ferred to in the report of gifts,nalusi.., y '3O reptiles and a fish,in exchange,"froin the Chadwick Museum,Bolton. The exchange had come about in a manner which re- fleeted great credit oa the condition of their Maseum. The authorities uf the Bolton Museum had in their pos- which was presented session a considerable number of reptiles which were unclassifiNl and nu-named. Having heard of the wi- lt: c rho: tfi reptiles lbe al\lr7aLrirainnasgta°su'. Greening, and which was perhaps the best collection in any provincial museum, the Bolton authorities asked that they might send their collection to Warrington to hive it classified and named. The collection came, and had been classi- fied, the work being undertaken almost entirely by a young man in the employ of the Museum Committee, named Mr. Lowe, a nattye of their own town, and who had developed great gifts in regard to natural history. In classifying the collection it was discovered that there were thirty reptiles which were not in the Warrington collection,and so an exchange was made. He mentioned this to show that.their Museum, although a small one, was rapidly coming to the front. He had noticed that terms to the con- dition of their exhbits, so that amongst other things they would SOJII have just cause to be proud of the con- dition af their Museum. (Hear, hear.) Councillor WOODS seconded the confirmation of the minutes. He wished to repeat what he had said at the committee,that they were getting on marvellously in the Library and Museum department, but in regard to art they were sticking fast. He had brought the matter i forward repeatedly n committee,and he load always been told to go to Mr. Roberts. He thought that now they were going to have an industrial exhibition at some- body else's risk they should carry out the art exhibition. If they did not do so,Warrington would sink in the worldesti- t hcoo membersn st de r a bl conjunction with the ex-Maynr, to get good representa- tive works of the leading artists of the day. This was an opportunity for Mr. Roberts to give them a whisper rhae trf efforts the someart of of what he intended to do as regards the art exhibi• tion. Councillor BENNETT asked why the matter of the Art Exhibition was not on the iinutes. He was at a loss to understand the committee's attitude in the matter ; they bad been playing at this art exhibition longer than the industrial exhibition, and they seemed to be paving the way for a fiasco. He did not understand what there was standing in the way of the realisation of an art exhibition. Councillor H. ROBERTS said the matter of the art ex- hibition had not been brought before the General Pur- poses Committee, as It perhaps Ought to have been, He pleaded guilty to the fact that at the last meeting of the committee he forgot to bring it forward. At the previ- ous meeting of the Council they were asked to get an estimate of what the cost would be. They had not been able to get the estimate because Messrs. Agnew could not give it. They could only say what similar exhibi- tions had cost in other places. It had been his intention to ask the General Purposes Committee to give the Museum Committee a cirque on Neje own responsi- bility for the amount estimated for thee purpose of the exhibition. The minutes were then confirmed INCREASE OF THE_CEwer, -:----TEHT REGISTRAR'S

It was resolved, at a meeting-Of tho Cemetery Com- mittee, that the salary of Mr. Robert Young, the regis- a r increased to a maximum of £l5O per annum, at an annual m ual increase of LlO, until the maximum be t rn a, 6 reached. Councillor EVAN 3 moved the adoption of the minutes, and said the only resolution it was ne3essary to refer to was that by which it was proposed to incroase Mr. young's salary. Thee proposed be should have an annual increase of LIO a year until the maximum of Ll5O per annum had been reached. The committee thought he was entitled to that sum. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Samtcocx seconded, and the motion was agreed to without comment. THE MARKE INSPECTOR'S SALARY.
The Markets Committee recommended that the salary of Mr. Elijah Place,as inspector of weights an 1 measures be increased by 53. a week as and from the 31st March next.

Alderman HUTCHINSON moved the confirmation of the minutes of the committee, and said there was nothing particular to refer to except the resolution as to Mr. Place's salary. Councillor SMETHURST : Nothing particular ! (Laugh- ter.) Alderman HUTCHINSON' (continuing) slid the salary waq to be increased by Si. a week. 'file committee were quite unanimous in the matter. Councillor WOODS Seconded, and the motion was agreed to. INCREASE OF GAS OFFICIALS' SALARIES.

- --------• The Gas Committee at a meeting held on the 14th January, adopted resolutions proposing to increase the salary of Mr. F. Taylor,the secretary, to a maximum of £250 per annum,by an annual increase of £lO. It was also resolved that the salary of Mr. W. S. lloward, the cashier,be increased to a maximum of £23o.and that of Mr. E. J. Smith,the chief clerk, to a maximum of £l5O at the same increase per year. Alderman leAramouna moved the confirmation of the minutes. LTA remarked that all the other motions for the increase of salary had gone on swimmiugly, and he hoped the resolutions now submitted would be equally successful. Mr. Howard had received no increase since 1888. He was appointed in Mr. Cooper's place. Since Mr. Howard had been appointed the work of the office had increased very considerably ; in fact, the receipts from the sale of gas now were £B,OOO a year more than
