Councillor H. Bonanza : But the Alderman--
_ Alderman SUTTON : I shall object because I have not finished.
The MAYOR : Councillor Itaberts is entitled to speak on the minutes. Alderman Surrost : Not on the remark I have been

making. (Laughter, and cries of " Chair," " chair.") Councillor H. ROBERTS : I claim a privilege,as state- ments have been made by the Alderman which are abso- lutely inc. )erect,and I claim a right of reply. I won't keep the Council more than five minutes. The Mayon : Is it the wish of the Council to hear Councillor Roberts? (General cries of "No, no," and " Yes, yes.") Councillor Loscrros: It is against the interests of the town to discuss the matter. Councillor Titssiox : It would be in the interests of public that we should have the other side of the state- ment. It is no use having a false impression. Let us have the truth. The Pdavon : If you will take my advice you will let the matter drop till the next Council meeting, when we shall have more information to lay before you. Councillor H. ROBERTS: It is not fair tat statements should go forth that the matter has been grossly neg- lected, and that we hive left the tenants in the cold. I say distinctly that it would have been better if someone else than Alderman Sutton had raised the question, be- cause he has appeared before the committee as agent of the property involved. Alderman SUTTON : I have nev'r appeared before the committee in such a capacity. Councillor Et ROBERTS: The Town Clerk has a state- ment of claim with respect to one of the properties in Bridge-street, made out by Alderman Sutton. Alderman SUTTON : Quite right. Councillor H.ROBERTS : Then if he is not the agent for the property, in what capacity is ha ? He has no right to speak at all. Toe reason the properties have not been purchased is that the committee considered the claims to be exorbitant, these are the figures :—Wilson's executors for the Feathers Hotel, £IB,OOO ; Alderman Cnandlev, £B,lOO ; Executors of Sutton.£7.9oo ; Execu- tors of John T0ft,26,000 ; Rowlinson,2l,2oo. Alderman SUTTON : I object to this. You never con- descend to make any negotiations at all with us. The MAYOR: It is quite time the discussion was closed. The ratepayes are not being benefited by the discussion. Councillor 11. ROBERTS : We want the ratepayers to know the difficulties we have to contend with. Our valuation comes to a little more than one-third of the amount claimed. This is our position. The discussion then dropped, and the minutes were agreed to. A NUISANCE IN WINWICK MEM'.

In accordance with notice given, Councilor Shaw Green moved that the urinal near the Lord Rodney in Winwick-street be removed. He remarked that he had received two letters from residents in the neighbourhood of the urinal complaining strongly of the nuisance in consequence of it. Alderman FRANCOMB seconded the proposition. Councillor EVANS said if it was removed there would be no public convenience between the Horse and Jockey and Bewsey-road. There was a great difficulty in ob- taining suitable sites.

CaUTICIIIOr PEACOCEE expressed himself strongly in favour of the removal of the urinal. It was nothing but a nuisance, and there had been serious complaints res- pecting it. It would be a mistake to spend any money on improving the present place. Councillor SMETHURST said the present condition of the place was a disgrace to the town. He was, however, of opinion that if the Council dispensed with it, another one should be fixed somewhere in the vicinity. Councillor F. R. ROBEEtTS referred to the conspicuous position of the urinal, and to the fact that it WAI overlooked by a great number of business places, and by the people who had to live there. It was their duty to insist on its being in a less conspicuous place. Councillor Joiato Ronnwrs also characterised the posi- tion as most unsuitable.

Councillor WOODS suggested that it should be placed underground. Councillor LONGTON said it was a great public: con- venience, and he was not in favour of its removal. On the vote being taken the motion was carried, Mr. Longton being the only dissentient. SHOULD WARRINGTON BE A COUNTY BOROUGH ? INFORMATION TO BE OBTAINED: Councillor HENRY ROBERTS moved "That the Town Clerk be instructed to prepare a Report at the earliest possible moment as to the desirability of Warrington be- coming a County Borough, and that he be further authorised to obtain such assistance as he may consider necessary for the purpose," He said the Council would notice that his proposal was absolutely of a non-com- mittal character. It was simply an instruction to the Town Clerk to prepare a report for the purpose of enabling the Council to stat.• whether Warrington shall be a County Borough or not. He was bound to say that personally, he felt very strongly that the time had come when they should take the necessary proceedings to be- come a County Borough.. At present they were subject • to the control of the County Council on several matters which bore very seriously on their position is a Borough. The Council was well aware of the conditions under which they in Warrington laboured in regard to technical instruction, and ha did not intend to enter Into detail. Every member was aware of the disabilities inflicted upon Warrington by the County Council in the manner of the amount of grant which was doled out to them for technical instruclon purposes. That would be removed if Werringten became a County Boroueh. It was also perfectly fresh within the memory of the Coun- cil as to the manner of the treatment of Warrington by the County Council only a few days ago with regard to the bridge question. But these in themselves would net be sufficient to justify Warrington beceming a County Borough. When the Local Government Act was passed the House of Parliament considered that a borough of 50,000 inhabitants was of sufficiently great importance to be a borough constituted with the powers of a County Council, and having control of its own affairs. Uniortunately at the time Warrington was not quitep to from people.lue s thantehaer , /15500e*,a000r0.00) to apopulation of over 62,000 limit,but since then it had grown was of the greatest importance that they should have the fullest possible amount of self-coatrol,and that they should have the least possible amount of outside interference. (Hear, hear.) County Councils generally were seeking additional powers to those they already possessed—and by County Councils be also meant County Boroughs. They were seeking t 3 have conferred upon them Soma the powers which the Local Government Board at present possessed, and if these were granted, Warrington in its present position weuld be subject to an extension of the outside control by the County Council. There was the question ef secondary education which was equally as important as elementary education, and it was proposed to confer on County Councils and County Borotighs the powers and authority which would have reference to the manage- ment of this subject. It was of the utmost importance that these powers should be placed in the hands of the authorities of the town. As te the question of finance, the Council was to some extent in the dark, but he - strongly of opinion that they bad nothing to fear on that ground. The basis of the present rateable value would be taken as the basil; of calcelation in relation to the , was financial adjustments between the Council and the County Council. He looked forward to a very consider- able expansicn of the rateable value of Warrington within the next few years. He did not think any of them had previously seen such a prospect of continued prosperity as seemed in front of Warrington at the pre- sent time, and it was of the utmost importance that none of the improved rateable value that Warrington might acquire should be added to the rateable value which the basis of I calculation will be made as between the County Council and themselves. He believed they had everything to I gain financially by making their arrangements at the present time instead of putting them off when the basis , of calculation might be doubled. These were the rea- sons which had prompted him to bring forward the re- ; se,lution, and from what he had heard he theught the Council would unanimously support it. (Applause.) Councillor BeerNarr seconded, and said the position I taken up by the County Council with reference to the bridge question gave the Council no other alternative but to endeavour to become a County Borough. The utter absurdity of proposing to to 30 feet when there were five widen ve roads, three of which on o eof t 3obridgefe et would be 60 feet wide, sod two others 50 feet, making 280 of street space converging n a bridge h e res proved conclusively that the County Council were ignor- ant of their requireneents,and not anxious to meet their wishes. He had no doubt that the reeert would furnish them with all particulars, and the Council would then be able to go into the question quietly and fully. Councillor SHAW GREEN said be was thoroughly in sympathy with the resolution proposed by Councillor Roberts, hut he would like to suggest that the name of Borough Treasurer be added to that of the Town Clerk in preparing woul d um the report. Be thought these two gentle- menable to give them all the information re- quired. Councillor Gams said the borough Treasurer had all the information at his disposal. Soma time ago he (Councillor Grace) wrote to him for a return of all the monies received by the town from the- County Council. The average amount received had been £3,500 per annum, The MAYOR I think it would be better to go into the figures at the committee meeting. Councillor Gila (continuing) said he had it from an

jauthoritative source that the amount received by tht County Council for Inland Revenue receipts from Wa rington in 1896 was £7.815 9s. 4. It was therefore clear that Warrington had only been receiving about 40 per cent of the money remitted from Warrington, and that. he contended, was not a fair per centage. W rington would be in a far better position if it were a county borough. Alderman SUTTON did not think it would be advisable for the Council to spend much money upon the report, and he was of opinion that the Town Clerk and the borough Treasurer would be able to furnish all the in- formation required, without getting outside assistance. Councillor Bonswrs said in drafting the resolution in the way in which was drawn he had in his mind the fact that the Town Clerk was the principal responeible officer, and he was the proper person to prepare the re. port. It was understood that he would make the report after consultation and in conjunction with his colleagne the Borough Treasurer, particularly inasmuch as he wag the chief financial officer. It might be necessary to ob- tain additional assistance beyond that in the possession of the Corporation officials. It was a question whicb resolved itself chiefly into one of finance. The County Council would be able to engage financial experts, and it behoved the Council to be as prepared as they were. It was of the greatest importance that the report should be prepared with the utmost exactness, even if they bad to employ experts lathe work. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was adopted with the inclusion of the name of the Borough Treasurer. The Council then rose.

div.head: WAS IT THE EARL'S DOG?
div.p: WAS IT THE EARL'S DOG?

WAS it not Pascal who said that if Cleopatra's nose had been an inch longer or shorter it might have changed the course of history P Very likely, inasmuch as history is nothing under the sun but a tale about vast numbers of people. And what alters the direction of one life may easly affect millions. You have, no doubt heard the story about the Earl of Wiltshire's dog. It was at the time the divorce of Henry VIII. was under discussion at Rome. Things were progressing favour- ably, and when the Pontiff, at the close of the audience pat oat his foot to be kissed by the Earl, the dog—whh had followed his master into court—bit it. This so en- raged the Pope and horrified the officials present that the negotiations were broken off. This story may be time or not, but we are all aware that the course of history was changed about that time. Such things merely illustrate the truism that you never can judge of the Importance of anything by the size of it. A nod of the head or a wink of the eye does sometimes literally and truely " speak volumes." On a tense harpstring it needs only the touch of a finger to elicit a tone loud enough to fill S. Paul's Cathedral ; and just an and- dental word or twe, dropped in passing conversation, may, all unbeknown to the parties speaking,be a matter of life or death to one or both of them. If,for instance, a womaa living in his town had not given a sensible bit of advice to James Ward he would never have written the letter setting forth the reason of it. In what way this chance talk affected him we will now see.

"In January, 1893," he says, "my health began to INI n”. I felt weary, tired, and weak, and could not think what had overtaken me. With the least exertion I was exhausted and perspiration poured off in'. After eating I had intense pein across the chest and stomach. A fixed throbbing pain settled in my left side (on the lower part of the ablomstAgiving me much trouble and uneasiness. Al my food turned sour on my stomach and gaseous wind would rise up into my throat and head, causing a lightness of the head, and for a time, luring each attack, I had to press my temples to ease " I soon got so low, weak, and dejected that I could' not attend to business properly. A laorrid, nervous feel. jog prevented ins sleapiag,and my c)ndition was sects that I did not care what became of me, and I despaired of ever being well again. For over two years I con. tinned like this. I consulted a docter,but was no better for any medicine that I took. In Ja1y,1893, Mss Jones at the Ste tar,Rostrevor,recernmeeled rn3 to try My.her Seigel's Curative Syrup. "I began taking this rue dieiae, and after taking the first bottle I lo•-• 11 to mend. My food no longer gay me pain, and t rain at my side was easier. I con- tinued with it, and emu I felt strong, all the wretched nervousness and sinking feeling leaving M 9. Since that time I have kept in good health, taking an 03C taloned dose of the medicine when required. You can make any use you like of this etetement. (Sigue I) Jams Ward Restravor, co. Down, Ireland, August 18th, 1897." Mr. Ward is a tailor i. business at Rostrevor, where he has resided many years. He is well known and res- pected throughout the district. HJ strongly recom- mends NS Wier Seigel's Syrup to all his friends and cus. tomers. It has often been observed of shoe nakers and tailors that they are apt to be unusually intellectual and thoughtful 'nee. The reason for this I will le ive the reader to finl oat for himself. They are also apt to be troubled with dyspepsia. watch may possibly be due to the contracted and canfined pesitions in which they work. Taen, too, they get bat vary little exercise, and exercise is a great stimulant to the digestion, Fro= these causes, acting, maybe with others that he does not mention, Mr. Ward's trouble arose. That it should have weakened him is plain to see, for strength deper. Is al- together upms ttae amount of nutritious food one eat, and is able to digest. Nothing will do in place of that.. and when Mr. Ward's victuals turned sour on his stomach ths source of his strength was cut off. Out of the fermentation of food within him came all the paing he speaks of, and the " Horrid nervous feeling "which reale him reckless and despairing as to his future.

ss Western Telegraph." of January 1, 1898 "Few houses in Manchester occupied in the same line of business are better known or enjoy a larger share of patronage than tlsat of Samuel Pitts, late of Gaythorn, now oflLondon-road, Manchester, the complete house shop, and office furnisher. It was In 1846 that the present proprietor initiated the business, operations having been first com- menced by him in Brook-street as a cabinet maker and dealer in °Mee furniture. By his energy and ability the concern prospered, and more acoomruodation becoming necessary, a move was made to the late premises in Gayttsern about 26 years since. Samuel Pitts soon Required a name for the superior excellence of the goods he supplied, the vast range of selection offered to customers, and the house advanced with rapid strides into a foremost and leading position in the trade. Just recently the Corporation purchased the Gay- thorn premises for streetimprevement purposes, and Samuel Pitts bad once again to find 'fresh fields and pastures new.' This time his choice fell upon the vast edifice until latterly known as Borough Buildings, situate 100 to 120. London-read, which he has now converted Into what is often termed the largest and most convenient general furnishing establishment in Man- chester. The premises occupied are enormous in extent and attractive in appearance, and are prominently and com- mandingly located. They comprise a magnificent frontage of plate-glass windows, well stocked with high-class goods, together with extensive showrooms nearly 300 feet long on the ground floor, and offices and counting house. The first, second, and third floors are occupied by a number of stock and showrooms, and extended workshop accommadation Is offered by the premises on the opposite side of London-road. The establishment throughout has been admirably arranged, and thoroughly and elegantly fitted up with every require- ment, including electilo light throughout, hydraulic pas- senger and luggage lift to all ilaors, for the effective display of the splendid selection of goods, which cannot be surpassed by those of any competitor, either in extent, variety, or general superiority. In soundness of material, good work- manship, and elegance and novelty of d,.sign the house has no successful rivals in Manchester, while prices will always be found of the moat satisfactory character. The proprietor Is thoroughly acquainted with every eligible source of supply and in addition to his own special make the establishment displays the choicest specimens, both new and second-hand, of other well-known manufacturers. Samuel Pitts is a thoroughly practical man, and his personal supervision is bestowed upon the business in its entirety, He is able, ener- getic,and courteous in his control, and all his dealings are marked by his methods of strict fairness and honesty. In conclusion, we should strongly advise all furnishing, whether in part or throughout, to pay this establishment a visit. The same civility and courtesy is extended to all, whether buying or not, and the firm's well known straightforward. syste- matic method ensures all orders being satisfactorily este- cut 131 ITTS'S HOUSES OF' PURNITUIIIi at 151, 221, 28f, 38:1, 50, 75,100, up to 1,500 guineas are still unrivaded, Full particulars and testimonials on applicit on, Cash price quoted ; deferred payment by arrangement. div.head: TUE EX A MINER.
div.p: TUE EX A MINER.
FEBRUARY 4th, 1898.

TnE supporters of the G overn- Foreign Affairs. ment seem to be suffering from a fit of depression at the pre- sent time. That section of them which is most infected with Jingorism is particular'y uneasy. Foreign affairs are not developing in the way they would like to see. Some of those Tory Jin- gos appear to have arrived at the conclusion that it is high time this country went to war with Somebody in some part of the globe. And it may be explained here that, as a rule, a Jingo's concep- tion of war is that he should do all the shouting at home while somebody else does all the fighting ittid endures all the hardships abroad. The re- ports from the Indian frontier have not satisfied his appetite for warlike views. In fact, he finds the latest details of the inglorious and disastrous '1 conflict with the frontier tribes decidedly distaste- Ail reading, although this "little war" is the direct outcome of the unnecessary and unwise "forward policy" in India 'which has been preached in season and out of season by British Jingos since the time of Lord BIDACONSFIRLD. What the Jingos now appear to want is that the Government should fly at higher and, for prefer- ence, more submissive game than the Afridis and other tribesmen. Within the last few weeks they have been encouraged to hope that the Govern- ment had at last determined to take a strong line in foreign policy. As everyone now knows Germany has seized a Chinese port and territory with a view to using it for the purposes of trade. Another csuntry—Russia—has of late been making even greater inroads upon the indepen- dence of China, and it is needless to say that where Russia rules there British trade is prac- tically annihilated by prohibitive tariffs. British trade with China is of a great deal more value and importance than that of all other European Countries put together. Here then was a Perfectly legitimate opportunity for Lord SALISBURY to assert the rights of this country in China in tho face of either RusQia or Germany,for British trade and British influence in the oast of Asia are inseparably bound up with each other. It has been understood all along that Lord SAMS- 33uRr had made it clear to China, and through China to all other countries concerned, that, in connection with any re-arrangement of Chinese territory, this country would not tolerate any Preferential treatment being accorded to other Powers in matters of trade. In taking up that Position Lord SALISBURY was on perfectly firm ground, forhe was 'backed up by treating obliga- tions, and he was supported by the leaders of Liberal opinion in this country as well as by his Own party. It was generally believed that on this occasion Lord SALISBURY had, for once, put his foot down firmly and had no intention of raising it again unless his terms were conceded. One of his conditions was that, if Russia obtained exceptional influence in northern China or Man- churia, the town of Ta-Lien-Wan should be made a free and open port. Yet, what is the latest news from the Chinese capital? To the amdzement of of everybody and to the consternation of his own Party, it is announced that Lord SALISBURY has once more given way in the facs of foreign pros- eau,. The demand that Ta-Lien-Wan should be "ea and open port has it is said, been with- drawu because Russia is determined to have her Own‘" this news be true its seriousness from a national and especially from a commercial point of view cannot be over-rated. It can only be des- cribed as the beginning of the end of British in- fluence in China, and s eme of its effects will 800/1 be seen in the diminu- tion of trade with that part of the world. P°ol3lo are now anxious to know the reasons for this great and unexpected surrender of important national interests. Is it due to the weakness

which seems to be inherent in Lord SALISBURY'S management of foreign affairs, or has a conces- sion been made in some other quarter which, in the opinion of the Government, is equivalent in value to the original demand? The country is certainly not prepared to hear with any degree of patience that the point has been yielded in defer- ence to the threats of foreign Powers. Explana- tions will now be awaited with the keenest in- terest, but in any case it must be clearly evident to the dinges of this country that Lord Sixissuity is not the man to suit their purposes.

How long will the "Union of The" Union of the of the Unionists" now re- Unionists." remain in existence? After the proceedings at Birmingham this week, it will surely not be long before Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and those who have finally determined to go with him throw off the last vestige of the Liberal cloak I which they have used to cover their renunciation of the whole Liberal creed. The seat at Birming- ham which has been rendered vacant by the death of Mr. GEORGE Dixon, one of the most Liberal of the Liberal-Unionist members of the House of Commons, has been handed over to the Tory party. This surrender of principal seems to have caused a great deal of annoyance to the Birming- ham Liberal Unionists, and the humiliation they have suffered will be none the less bitter because it has been practically forced upon them by Mr. cumsrBERTAT.N. The incident should have some useful results. It must, one would think, finally convince those Liberal Unionists who still cling to some at least of their Liberal convictions that there is now practically no difference between Liberal Unionism as expounded by Mr. CHAMBER- um and downright Toryism. In fact, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN himself is getting into a way of talking to his hitherto submissive followers in Birmingham in a tone which can scarcely be distinguished from that of some of the most out- spoken Tories who have never professed any for Liberal Unionism. He tells 1d even in Birmingham, which they have them mat that regarded as their citadel, they would be quickly wiped out as a political force if it were not for the support of the Tories and in the course of the little speech he addressed to the members of the Edgbaston Liberal Unionist Divisional Council he twice threatened to resign his official connection with their association if they did not support the Tory nominee. But in face of this dire threat there were still no fewer than twenty-nine of the delegates who voted against the acceptance of the Tory yoke. There I should now even in the capital of the Midlands be a clearing of the political atmosphere. Mr. CnAmmtntairr endeavoured tor several years to keep up the delusion that he was still as good a Liberal as anybody on nine out of the ten articles in any Liberal programme, but there have been not a few signs lately to show that he is aware the part is now played out. All his enthusiasm for domestic reforms has vanished, and he is in tbe habit of evoking Tory cheers by declaiming about the grandeur of the Empire in the vein of that much-neglected politician, Sir ASHMEAD BARTLETT. After the object-lesson at Birming- ham this week it may, we believe, be taken for granted that Liberal Unionism as an organised force disappears from the politics of this country.

Apparently there are, even yet, people sanguine enough to believe that the Ship Canal is not the hopeless failure from a revenue-producing point of view, that many would have us believe. And, curiously enough, an energetic and commonsense defence of the great undertaking comes from a London critic, who has aired his views in the" Pall Mall Gazette." After describing the extent to which railway and shipping combinations have retarded the success of the Canal, he says it must of neces- sity arrive at a period of financial prosperity unless it is overtaken by bankruptcy before that period is reached. The danger of this contingency he lessens by the argument that the predominant owners of the Canal are the citizens of Manchester —not the shareholders—and this fact he considers a practical guarantee of the undertaking's solvency. And this is not all. Tee writer fears not to tackle that bugbear of hope and confidence—the deprecia. tion of shares.Thisconstant dropping of share-prices, until both ordinary and preference shares are now under .£1 in value has been freely used as an argu- ment against any prospect of the Canal's betterment, and to the uninitiated has proved unanswerable. 1 The London writer styles the importance given to it as exaggerated and asserts that there is no busi- ness worthy of the name, done in Canal shares. " Well-to-do shareholders " he says, "will not part with their shares at present prices, and at the same time they do think it worth while to increase their holdings by the few shares which stress of circum- stances(abnormal this year owing to labour troubles) compels the smaller shareholder to put upon the market. The only market upon whice this small shareholder can rely upon for his shares is among the limited class who are will- ing to acquire a few Canal shares so as to be able to say that they have an, interest in theundertaking. Upon therefore transactions amounting to a few hundreds the value of millions has been appraised, and the decision to sell arrived at in a few back parlours isiconsidered suficient justification:for' writ ing the word failure on an undertaking that but four years ago was considered of such national importance as to justify Her Majesty the Queen conferring the honour of opening it herself in person." We are pleased to see the position of affairs looked at from so hopeful a standpoint and would fain believe in the prediction that " success must be eventually attained,and the enterprise and sacrifices of those who have made Manchester a seaport, rewarded."

SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN. INQUEST AND VERDICT. Mr. J. E. Wortley held an inqueat on Tuesday at the Runcorn police station touching the death of Ann Dang- le% aged 29, who resided with her husband at No. 1, Cawley-et., and who died suddenly on Monday morning. Llewellyn D)uglas, the husband, said of late his wife had not been very well and had complained of pain in her stomach and side. A doctor called on one occasion but as their blinds were down he went away again. Witness had repeatedly asked her to see some one and last week she promised she would go and see Dr. Robin- son. On Sunday'night they had a supper of turnips, potatoes and .old mutton. The decoased had eaten very heartily and retired to bed about 10.40. She did not disturb him during the night but in the morning he awoke to find her sitting up in bed. When he was Just going to ask her what was the matter she fell hack in his arms. Ho held her there until he thought she was recovering, and was then going to lay lay her down when she appeared to hive taken a second fit. Ho afterwards laid her down and went and called Mrs. Stubbs, a neighbour. From the time that he found her sitting up in bed to the arrival of Mrs. Stubbs it would be about half-an-hour. Witness got morn, brandy, but he could not get her to take it, and he then went for Dr. Ormsby. R 5 came immediately and pronounced life to be extinct.

In answer to the Coroner, witness said that on one occasion during the ight the little boy was uncovered, and after covering him up she said, "I think we have all had a bit too enech simper." The deceased bad bad alit about thr.- weeks ago, but she bad come quickly out of it.fihe afterwards said that " fainty bouts" made ' her very ill. Sarah Frances Stubbs said she had known the de. ceased for many years, but had known her very inti- mately since Whitsuntide. She appeared to be in a very poor state of health, and often complained after having a meal or after having over-exerted herself. She bad mentioned to witness the fact that she had had a fainty bout about three weeks ago. She said Mr. Douglas bad told her it was not a natural fainty bout, more like a fit. Witness told her she ought to see a doctor, but she seemed to have an objection to doctors. Witness had seen her in a fainty bout before. Witness was called to the house of the deceased on Monday morning. In wit- pass's opinieti she was dead then, as she found it im- possible to bring her round. Dr. Orproby deposed that be was called in on Monday morning to are the deceased and found her dead. Wit- ness thought she had suffered from heart disease for some time and that would make her suffer from indi- gestion after meals. He thought it very probable that the heavy meal she had the night before might have been the means of producing the fatal result owing to the weakness of the heart. The cause of death was heart disease. There were no marks of violence on the body. In witness's opinion she ought to have been un- der medical treatment.
The jury returned a verdiet in accordance with the medical testimony.

DROWNING FATALITY AT RUNCORN. THE CORONER AND A WITNESS. Mr. J. C. Woreley held an inquest on Tuesday, at the Runcorn Police Station, toueking the death of Frank Kelly, aged 27 years, who resided at 25, Byrom-street, and who was found drowned in the Bridgewater Canal on Sunday. Thomas Murphy, 25, Byrom-street, said the deceased was his brother-in-law and be was a chemical labourer. Witness last saw him alive about half-past six on Satur day evening. He was then going to Widnes where be made a practice of goinfr on Saturday nights. Thomas McCormack, Barn-street, Widnes, said he last saw the deceased on Saturday night at 11 o clock. He left him at the corner of Barn-street, talking to some young women. He was quite sober when witness left him. He had had some ale but was not drunk. Witness had also had some ale but was not drunk. By Superintendent : Witness remembered tell. jog P.C. Gregpry the previous night that the deceased was drunk. in answer to a juror witness said the deceased was quite able to take care of himself. John Rawlinson, lock tenter at N. 3, Lock on the Bridgewater Canal said on Sunday morning same time near one o'clock be heard some one moaning in the water. Witness got the boat hook and on going to the place where he heard the moaning he heard a gurgling noise. Witness dragged the boat book up and down and found a cap. It was raining at the time. In witness's opinion the deceased has been taking a short cut home. Peter Johnson said about 10 o'clock on Sunday morn- ing he commenced grappling operations. When the body was recovered information was given to the P.C. Gregory stated that he had examined the body , of the deceased and had found no marks of violence. On the deceased was found an old knife, is. lid., two clay pipes and a piece of tobacco, Witness had made in- quiries and had found that when he came over Runcorn Bridge he was drunk, and that he had refused to give up his ticket. I The Coroaer asked if he had heard anything about the persons who were said to have heard the deceased moan- ing. Witness eaid a Mrs. Finneys lived about ten yards dis- I tance from the canal. They were all in bed. They came down stairs. but of course, it was all over then. A Juror: It is a most singular thing that the lock tenter did not hear the deceased. Tup said no doubt the decehaesedC:ras"r n drunk when rnieg came across the bridge from Widnes. His opinion was, that he was finding his way by what was supposed to be a near cut when begot into the canal. The jury returned a verdict of "Found Drowned." Thomas McCormack asked the Coroner if he could be allowed any expenses as he had lost a day's work. The Coroner : If you come to tell untruths like you havesu p rtolditeo_day you will loose more than that. nt ndent O'Kell : Why did you not tell the e truth. McCormack : I eid. Superintendent O'Kell : ICY-1 no you didn't. McCormack then left the court.

RUNCORN LIBERAL :CLUB. ANNUAL MEETING: The annual meeting of the members of the above club w el ay on g at the club premises, lieags held mMr.onAd.lt.e=rlilan presided over a good attendance. THE ANNUAL REPORT, The Secretary, Mr. A. Riley,read his annual report as follows ;—ln presenting a report of for the year 1897 it is satisfactory to be able to state that after meetin. all the expenditure of the year the income has allowed' the ' club building account to be reduced by the sum of £2O 17e. 21, which now stande at the comparatively small amount of £268 153. CI. Daring the year considerable alterations and renewals have been made in the club r remises including the in- stallation of incondescent lighting, and though these im- provements have enti.:led a considerable cost,they have greatly added tc the attractiveness of the club and the comfort of the members, which it N hoped will induce many of the younger members of the Liberal party to join the club and add to its usefuiness. During the year the club has chiefly devoted its energies to its social work, and a number of billiard matches with neighbouring clubs have been played and which have no doubt encouraged kindly feelings and extended acquaintance with those of other constituences, who,while divided by dietarice,are at one with us in aim and work as members of the great Liberal parry. These interchanges of courtesies have necessarily entailed a somewhat greater cost than formerly, but this is more than counterbalanced by the memory of many pleasant evenings and tie widening of our sympathies. The year's income including the balance of £5 63. Id. brought forward at its commencement has been £lB9 14s. 4d., and the expenditure £l5B 17s. 21., leaving as stated previously the sum of £2O 17s. 21. which has been applied to the reduction of the amount owing on the club premises. A club social took place on the evening of February 22ad, a small special committee ably undertaking all the arrangements. It is needless to say that a very happy and pleasant evening was thus spent, many 0 the members contributing by song and speech to the general enjoyment. More frequent gatherings of this kind would doubtless promote those social feelings which add so much to the pleasure of living, and the enjoyment of members. In tho early part of the year Mr. J. W. S. Callieteecre- tary of the Financial Reform Association, lectured on "The Financial relations between Great Britain and Ire• land." fie was accompanied by Mr. ft. McGhee M.P. A great mass of useful and iestructive information was imparted and a very pleasant and profitable even- ing was thus spent. Owing to the available dates not being suitable to the lecturers with whom it was hoped that arrangements would be made, no lectures were given during the year, but it is hoped that during the course of this year additional lectures may be given hav- ing for their purpose ,the spread of Liberal principles thus preparing fur the triumph ol the Liberal party and its return to power as the result of the next general elec- tion. div.head: RUNCORN COUNCIL AND ITS DRAINS.
div.p: THE RUNCORN COUNCIL AND ITS DRAINS.

London and North-Western Railway and Great Wes- tern Railway v. the Runcorn District Council,—ln the Chancery Division of the High Court, on Friday, before Mr. Justice Stirling, an application was made by the plaintiffs in this action to have an order confirmed, whereby the drains and ditches referred to in the suit, arid which the District Council contended were sewers within the meaning of the Public Health Act, and accordingly vested in them, ani described in the order made by the learned judge when the action was tried, some two months ago,as land-drains and ditches,whereas the District Council desired them to be described as sewers. Mr. Shearman appeared for the railway com- panies, and Mr, E. P. Hewitt represented the District Council. Mr. Hewitt said he was willing that the words should he" land-drains, ditches. or sewers," and not" land drains and ditches," as described by the railway com- panies in the order as altered by their counsel. Mr. Justice Stirling considered that Mr. Hewitt's con- tention was well-founded, and directed that the judg- ment should be in that torm, namely, 'land drains, ditcties, or sewers."
OUR LOCAL CRURCFIES. WARRINGTON eaRISEI CHURCH.

A service for men was held at the Parish Church on Sunday aP.ernoon. There was a fairly large coegrega- Lion. The Rev. A. Wright, secretary of the White Cross League, gave an address on "Toe Temple of the Body." The White Cross League Church of England Society em- bodied the effort to urd-e Christian mon on definite Church lines in the organised promotion of purity of life. This society is the same as the old Church of Eng- land Purity Society, its present name being suggested by the Archbishop of Canterbury, to avoid the appear- ance of opposition to the White Cross Society, but none of its Principles, methods, or officers were changed. It remains, what it has always been, a society of Church- men for the promotion of social purity.

The minutes were confirmed. At a later stage of the meeting it was decided to ad- vertise for an industrial trainer at a salary of £25 per annum with board and lodgings. It was understoo, that preference would be given to a person with a know- ledge of gardening. It was explained that the ',loll G Dvernment Bpard would re-pay a portion of the salary.

div.head: RUNCORN 'RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN 'RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of the above Council was held on Tuesday afternoon at Dutton Workhouse, Mr. J. Mc- Intyre, J.P., presiding. There were also present Messrs. J. Knowles, J. Stokes, J. Weir, T. Lewis, T. Wright, E. A. Wallington, J. Spruce, W. bolt, J. Parr, W. Brad- ford, S. Woodward. J. Spruce, J. Whitlow, J. B. Chad- wick, J. L. Jones. C. Mounfield, E. Bratherton, J. M. Williams, T. Baxter, Admiral Jones Parry, J. Ashton (clerk), G. F. Ashton (deputy clerk), J. Swinton, and Diggle (surveyors), and J.. Farrington (nuisance inspec- tor). PUBLIC WATER COMPANIES.

The Mailing Rural District Council forwarded the fol- lowing copy of a resolution they had adopted, and in- vited the Runcorn Rural District Council to adopt a similar resolution and urge the Local Government Board and their local reprevantative in Parliament to take ac- tive steps in the matter. " Tnat a representation be made to the Local Government Board with a view to re- gulations being issued,imposing the duty upon all public water companies to submit periodically at their own ex- pense an analysis of water supplied by them to all Dis- trict Councils (Urban and Rural) ; the mode of taking and submitting samples to be determined by the Local Government Board." . . .

Inspector Farrington said they had taken that pre- caution for years. The Sanitary Authority had paid for it themselves,and had never asked the company to pay. —The Chairman : This throws the cost upon the Water Companies.—Mr. Farrington : Yes.—The Council de- cided to support the resolution of the Mailing Council.

div.head: SANDY-LINE, PRESTON BROOK,
div.p: SANDY-LINE, PRESTON BROOK,

Mr. Spruce said when the question of footpaths was before the Council the meeting wag considerably influ- ence i by what Mr. Darbyshire said upon the matter. He (Mr. Spruce had gone into the matter once and he found that the repairs were done in 1889. Mr.Darbyshire told him that he was not in the service of the Highway Hard at that time. He found the Parish Councils Aor was permissive as to taking over footpaths, and he moved that Messrs. Baxter, Spruce, and Darlington be appointed a special committee to deal with the question of liability in reference to the repair of the footpath known as Sandy-lane, Preston Brook.

KINGSLEY WATER SUPPLY. Mr. Farrington reported that he had suhmitte d seve- ral samples of water to Mr. Carter Bell, county analyst. Samples had been taken from the public running pipe situate in" The Slack,"singsley,on January la h,and the analyst's remarks on it were :—" This is a good water, and fit for domi stic use." From the pump and well to "The Cedars" situate off Chester-road, in Helsby ; from public running pipe situate on Brook-side at end of Dark-lane, Kingsley ; and public runninE pipe near the lower end of Kingsley village, known as Plumbers' pipe. —The analyst reports on the latter three samples as fol- lows :—"Very good water, and fit for domestic use."— Mr. Farrington said the water supply within the Colin. cil's district compared very favourable with any other district in the county. The number of samples taken by the officer of the Runcorn Council was in excess of any other district in the nation.—The Chairman : It is very favourable indted. I am glad to hear it.—Mr. Woodward referred to reports that got about in refer- ence to water supplies and the sanitary state of various villages and townships in the county, and thought they should be verified before they were spread about. It was a most serious thing to attack the sanitary state or water supply of a village,:and he would like the Council to declare their opinion that such reports should be properly verified before they were made publie.—On the motion of Mr. Woodward a copy of the analyses was ordered to be sent to the County Medical Officer of Health. FINANCE.

Mr. Woodward reported that th 9 balance in hand after the last meeting WAS £1.29D 133. 1.1..1., and there had been receipts since of £lB2 24. 2d The payments that day amounted to £1,120 9i., leaving a balance in hand of £352 84. 81. This was all the businesS.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the above Board was held on Tuesday night,Mr, J. Pritchard presiding. There were also present the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., E. Imison, C.C., F. J. Norman, J.P., and G. Moss (clerk). scimor. ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. The School Attendance Committee reported that 80 parents had been summoned before them be breaches of the Education Act ;48 appeared, and proceedings were ordered to he taken against six. The visitors' report for the month ending January 21st showed that the total number of children on the school registers was 3,341, against 3,401,in January last year, decrease 80. The average attendance was 2,B4o,increase 47 compared with last year. The attendance had been unusually good for I a winter month, having reached 85 per cent. No doubt this was mainly attributable to the very mild weather land afforded evidence that there was no great amount 1 of sickness amongst children in the town.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. linison. The School Management Committee recommended for payment accounts amounting to £224 is. 4d., and that Mr. Albert E. Parr be appointed certificated as. sistant teacher at Brunswick Sena at at £75 pr annum ; and that Miss Sarah Marlow be appointrd assistant at Granville-street School, at £4O per annum.—Pad on the motion of Mr. Norman beconded by Mr. Taylor. This was all the business.

Lord Wolseley has a great objection to the system of " gate money" being charged for witnessing any athle- tic sports which take place on Government land,and an order has been issued to prevent a repetition of such practices throughout the service. La future the general officer commanding the regimental district is to give his approval or otherwise in special cases,which may be for charitable purposes. Bre., and some relaxation will be permitted in regard to the matter when a charge is made to cover expenses essentially connected with mili- tary sports.

div.head: LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY.
div.p: LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY.
THE INSPECTOR AND THE POOR RATE.

On Tuesday, in the Council Chamber of Runcorn Town Hall, Mr. Edmund Pearse fiord, an inspector of the Local Government Board held a public inquiry with respect to the application of the Runcorn Urban District Council for the issue of a provisional order under section 303 of the Public Health Act. 1875 to alter or amend the Runcorn Improvement Act, 1852 so as to make the lim- its of the urban district co-extensive with those of the township of Runcorn, by incorporating with the said district so much of the estuary of the river Mersey as was added to the township of Runcorn by the Poor Law Amendment Act, 1868. Mr. Walter C. Ryde, barrister at law, supported the application on behalf of the Urban Council, and there were present Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., E. bnison, C.C., W. Handley,T. Dean, F. A. Lake (law clerk) E. Marshall (secretary) J. Wilding(surveyor) M. Harker (consulting surveyor) W. Sutton (assistant overseer). Mr. Ryde explained that it was not desired Ito alter the boundary but to define it. The Poor Law I Amendment Act of 1868, Secti.m 27, defined the bound- [l 'tries of parishes on the banks of • tidal river to be the r middle of the stream, and the application of the District ICouncil was that the Local Government Board would bring their local Act of 1852 to the full limits of the General Act of 1868. There was absolutely no reason why this order should not be made. He put in a plan of the townships.

Replying to the Inspector, Mr. W. Handley said the portions of Halton added to Runcorn were quite sur- rounded by Runcorn. They were added tinder the Divided Parishes Act, 11184. The Inspector inquired if the boundary were settled with Widnes.

Mr. Lake said there was no question between them wri.l Widnes. Widnes was established under the Local Board Act, 1575. Their district probably followed the parish boundary. Mr. Handley displayed a map shoeing that the County boundary was the centre of the river.
Tha lespsctor said that was the same as the parish boundary...

M Wilding explained the plans. Mr. Lake stated that the district rate was 35. in the £ per annum ; and the poor rate Is. 2d. in the £ half yearly, The Inspector : It is a great deal too big then. Mr. Lake: lam sure we all agree with that. The Inspector : 2s. 41. in the a year for poor rate in this part of the world,is much out of all proportion. How much of this is county rate. Mr. Imisou : About 31.
Mr. W. Handley said there Wl9 also Burial Board rate in the poor rate. Mr. Marshall said the Burial Board rate was about 21. in the £ per annum.
Mr. itllBol3 : The School Board rate is the greatest tax upon the poor rate.

Mr. Handley : According to the last blue book the School Board rate is sd. for the year. It will b. 61. this year because the Board have ext.nded the school. Mr. Sutton said a penny on the poor rate produced 2205 nett.
Mr. Marshall said a penny on the district rate produced £lB2.
Mr. Lake said differential rating in connection with the docks made the difference.
There wa9 no opposition to the application and the In- spector Laid he would report to the Local Government Board.
RUSCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the above Council was held on Thursday morning in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, Runcorn, the vice-chairman, Mr.J.W.Light- burn, presiding. There were also present—Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C., E. Imison, C.C., W.Collier, G. H. Kirkham, J. Jones, J. Pritchard, T. Dean, J. Wilson,M. Sweetman, J. Horsefleld, G. Hewitt, D. Bisbrown, W. Handley, the Rm. Dr. Gast&ldi E.Marshall (secretary), F. A. Lake (law clerk), and J. Wilding, (surveyor).

div.head: THE. HEALTH OF THE TOWN-.
div.p: THE. HEALTH OF THE TOWN-.

Dr. McDougall in his report for the month of January stated that th, nunsber of deaths was 22. These deaths showed an averaze death rate for the twelve mouths of 15.08 and exclusive of the inquest cases of 13 07. Fifty six births were registered. Eighteen deaths and 43 births were registered for the corresponding month of last year.—The Chairman observed this was very satis- factory.

div.head: HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: HEALTH COMMITTEE.

It was recommended by this committee that fault having been found by the Surveyor with property, Ns. 43, 45 47. 49. and 51, Regent-strset, 1,3, Sankey's- court, 18. 20, Bridgewater-street, 7, Egerton-street, 21, 23, 25, Nelson-street, 5 and 7a, Regent-street, awl 9, Stanley-villas, instructions were given to the owners to remedy the same.—The minutes were adop"ed on the motion of Mr. Dean.

div.head: WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: WATER COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommended that four suits of water- proof clothing for the use of the men going down the well he obtained and that Mr. John Yates' tender bor supplying the same be accepted ; that the Runcorn reservoir be cleaned; and that th sum of £llB I3i. 2d. for empties, in respect of the water rate for the quarter ended Christmas Day, 1897, be written off—Mr. Pritchard proposed the adoption of the minutes and they were carried.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended that a rent of £l5 per annum be charged for :he use of the Cemetery Office about to be erected at the Town Hall, such rental to be a charge on the burials fund. (The rent to include beat- ing, lighting, cleaning, &-i.) ; and that the Chairman of the Committee, the Surveyor and the Secretary be authorised to purchase a typewriter.—Mr. Inaisin in proposing the adoption of the above minutes, referred to the first minute and said it was no new imposition and did not mean a fresh burden on the ratepayers.—The minutes were confirmed.
THE COUNTY COUNCIL TECHNICAL EDUCATION COMMITTEE
AND RUNCORN.

A letter was read fr-o-n-tt;;;Fe-cl-Mical Instruction Coin. mittee of the Cheshire County Council granting the Run- corn Technical Committee £5O nwards educational purposes for the current year.—The Chairman said he was very glad to say that it was an additional in- come which was not anticipated.—Mr. Speakman said he was very glad to hear that letter read. They were second to none in the county in technical education and ths County Council committee had ex- pressed that Runcorn were at the top of the tree. He would like to take this opportunity of saying that a great (Inal of this work was due to his colleague, Mr. unison, on the Technical Instruction Committte. They had endeavoured to obtain this £5O and had at last succeeded. • In addition to the £5O tnere was also a guinea for every scholar coming from rural districts, and he (the speaker) found that there were 16 from outside districts, and consequently that meant 16 guineas more. —Mr. unison said this secondary education seemed to be appreciated by the County Council, and this amount would be found very usefal.—Mr. Wilson said that he had known for some time that Mr. unison and Mr. Speakman had been doing their best to obtain this addi- tional money, and it was very pleasing to know that It was now an accomplished fact.—Mr. unison thanked the members for the words they haii uttered in regard to his and Mr. Speakman's services. He did not think that they had yet exhausted the County purse, and if they showed a good case they would get more assistance. (Hear, hear). The Council shortly afterwards rose.

PAINFUL CASE AGAINST A WARRINGTON YOUTH, On Thursday morning at the Warrington Borough Police Cow t,before Lieutenant-Colonel Ridgway and Mr. Jameaßeplerd,Willi.m flammond,a respectable looking youth of 20. was charged with committing an aggravated assault on El:zebeth LE e in a passage between Catherine- street and Pierpoint-st at 11 p.m. on Wednesday.—He pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable said this was a very painful case and he was as soriy as anyone else to see this young man in the position he was. Mrs. Lee was the wife of Thomas Lee, brakesman in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company. Alyut ten minutes to 11 on Wednesday night she went out to make a perchase and had to pass through an entry between Catherine-street and Pierpoint-street. When she reached the middle of the passage she was seized by the defendant who as- saulted her and made use of a foul expression. She screamed and her screams brought to her assistance a mei named John Wood, who followed defendant and gave him into custody in Folly-lane. P.C. Chrimes took him to the Police Station, where he gave a raise name. —Mr. A. Browne appeared for defendant,whose conduct he said was unaccountable to everybody. He was a teetotaller and his father was a most respectable man. There was nothing whatever against defendant's char- acter, and while he could not minimise the seriousness of the ewe he hoped the Bench would deal leniently with him as he had not been up before.—The Chief Con- seable said there was another case against defendant, the offence being committed in the same place on Decem- ber llth.—Defendant said he was repentant, but afered no explanation of his conduct.--The Chairman said this sort of thing was rather common both inside and cut- side the town. It must be put a stop to, and while they were very sorry for his father, they must make an ex- ample of defendant.He must go to prison for one month. A SERVANT GIRL'S DISEIONESTY.—THEFT OF A £25 RING. On Thursday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, before Lieutenant-Colonel Ridgway and Mr. J. Hepherd, Elizabeth Powell, a servant of Mrs. Pollitt, Orford Barrane s, was charged with stealing a diamond ring, value £25, between January 1 and February I. Ske pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable stated that the ring was stolen from the jewel ease of Mrs. Pollitt, wife of Captain Mitt, Orford Barracks. The girl had been in the service of prosecutrix for about 4 months, and on the Ist January Mrs.Pollitt took off her ring and put it in her jewel case. She had not cause to wear it again until February 1, when it was missed. Informa- ion was given tn the pence, and Detective-Inspector Monaghan and Detective Williamson interviewed the prisoner, who admitted taking the ring. She said she had a dress-piece being made up by a Mrs. Barry, and not having the money to pay for it she took the ring and gave it Mrs. Berry as a guarantee of payment. She was unaware of its value. Mrs. Berry, who was deli- cate, got an order for admission to a convalescent home at Southport, and being short of money, she took the ring to a shopkeeper in Latchford, a Mrs. Miller, who gave her an advance of ss. upon it. Both of them ap- peared to be ignorant of its real value. When the police went to the shop at Latchford they instantly received the ring. The Chief Constable added that a number of other articles had been missedond one or two traced to the prisoner. She had evidently been pilfering during the whole of her four months' service.—Mrs. Pollitt, the prosecutrix,Pleaded in tears with the Bench not to send the girl to prison. She said she was only 18.—The Chair- man said they could not overlo de the case, and prisoner must go to gaol for 14 days with hard labour.

div.head: MINOR CASES.

QUARRELS BETWEEN FUSTIAN CUTTERS—EIIen Davies, a girl about 16, 27 Winwick-road,. was charged with assaulting Florence Smythe, 2 Boardman 's-yard. on January 20th.— The evidence cn both aides showed that the parties (who were fustian cutter') were equally to blame and the case was dis- tnissed,—Jane Skelhotn. 46 Ctiorley-street, was summoned by Ellen Bolton, 14 Haydock-Areet, for assault. —The tins worked „t, the (+erne place as th9le in the previous case, and the Bench dismissed the ewe. A DRASTIC CHECK TO 1 DANGERCUS FRACTICE,—WaIter Jones. Black Lion Row, Wild.rspool. WAS charged with assaulting and beating Luther Allen, 2 Mersey-st., on Janu- ary 20.—Luther Allen, a small boy of about 12, said that on the day stated he had hold of the back of defendant's lorry with one hand. Jones came round and hit him in the face, making his nose bleed.—Defeudint sal 1 the boy was swinging on the lurry-box with his leg very near the wheel. He was afraid of an accident and attempted to box the boy's ears, but the latter turned round the same moment and received the blow on his nose.—The magistrates thought that defendant did quite right in sending the boy away from the lorry, but thought he had hit rather too hard. He was fined Is. includ- ing costs. THRESTS,—Blizabeth Marsden. 17 Alde.-lane, was charged with using threats to Hannah Hodgson. 1 Alder-lane, en January 21.—She admitted threatening to strike complain- ant.—Mr. Dsvies prosecuted, and detailed the circumstances of the case, which showed that complainant was in fear of defendant in consequence of the litter's behaviour.—Defend- ant was bound ova^ to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay Zs. 6d elate.

Crosileld had to employ three constables on their works in consequence of the wholesale robberies which used to take place there.— Warburton was allowed to go on a conviction being accorded against him. Shaw Green, A Row ow TOWN HlLL.—William Quinn, Town Hlll, pleaded guilty to a charge of being drunk and disorderly at 11-20 on Monday night.—P.O. Sankey said that be Was called to the scene of the row, and found prisoner in his house using obscene language and assaulting his wife. He was drunk and kicked his wife while she WBS on the ground.—Defendant pleaded his drunkenness as the cause of his behaviour. Not havitig a bad character, the bench only fined him be. and costs.

WEDNESDAL—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman), Mr. J. Geddes, Mr. T. Birchall. Mr. John Fairclough and the Mayor. DBITNIC AND DISORDERLY.—Tames Ellis was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horsernarket-street at 1145 on Tuesday nlgbt —P C. Clough proved the case and defendant was tined ss. and costs, _ .

. CHARGE aciairrar A HUSBAND.—Corrielius Ward, Morris'- court, Silver-street, was charged with assau ting and beat- ing his wife, Emily Ward, on January 29th.—Mr. Jenkins defended.—Mrs. Ward said that on Saturday night she wss coming up Pir nees-brow when she met her husband. She had some conversation with him and he called her foul names, following this up by thumping and kick- ing her. He kicked her in the fare and gave her two black eyes.—Hr. H. Taylor, Police Court Missionary, said that at the time in question he was coming up Winwicic-street, when he saw defendant rush at his wife and kick her twice. He appeared to be mai at the time.— Mr. Jenkins said that the conduct of the complainant had been abominable, and he was I:surprised that defendant had not done anything more serious. The complainant had been consorting with other men.—Mrs. Tnomason and her daughter deposed to have had a quarrel with Mrs. Ward, and both had struck her in the face. Mrs. Thomason said she , herself caused Mrs. Ward's black eyes.—The magistrates said that the assault had been proved, notwithstanding the extenuating circumstances. He was bound over to keep the peace and pay the costs 17s.
THU-RBDAY.—Before Lieutenant-Colonel Ridgway (chairman)
and Hr. J,Hepherd,

TEMPORARY AUTHORITY.—Dsvid Plinston was granted temporary authority to sell at the King's Arms, Buttermar- ket-st- in lieu of Edward Thompson. DEnERTIon OF FAMILY. --Edward Alcock was charged with mr fling away from the borough and leaving his wife and two children chargeable to the Warrington Union on June 28.—Mr. Basil Shearer, enquiry officer, prosecuted and said that prisoner's wife and two children were admitted to the Workhouse on June 28th for the second time. A warrant was taken out for his apprehension, and his family remarned in the Workhouse 33 days at a cost of £3 4s. 6d. On Wed- nesday night prisoner was apprehended at his mother's house in a state of intoxication.—The magistrates sent pri loner to gaol for a month's hard labour. THErr HY MEANS OF A TRICK —Alice Foulkes, last from St. Helens, pleaded guilty to a charge of stealing by means of a trick on Tuesday a silk handkerchief value ls. 9d. from the shop of Sarah Taylor, Priestley-st. —The Chief Constable related that on Tuesday afternoon prisoner came to Mrs. Taylor's shop and said that a customer of her's, Mrs. Ashen, had noticed in her shop window a silk handkerchief which she liked, and that she had sent her (prisoner) for it. She , selected one and said she would bring it back if it was not approved of. Prisoner pawned the handkerchief when she I got outside and was apprehended on Wednesday by P.C. Rylatt. She was in custody in St. Helens for a similar offence on January 27. and handed over to the Police Court Missionary who found her a home, but she left. —She was committed for 14 days hard labour. UNPROVOKED ASSAULT ON A CABMAN —A rough-looking farm labourer from Stretton named John Reid was charged with being drunk and ,db:orderly in Bridge-A. at 10.40 en Wednesday night and also with essatlting Richard Jinks in fty lands-at. the same night —Prisoner said he knew nothing about U.—Richard Sinks, cab driver, said he was on the rank in Rylands-st. on Wednesday night about 9.15 when prisoner came to him and struck him in the face without any provo- cation. He then went up the "Eagle and Child" yard and entered a stable, where witness locked him up and in- formed the police.—P.C. Clarke deposed to apprehending prisoner in the stable whare he was asleep. He refused to give his name and address and used filthy language He was very violent and it took three officers to get him to the Pollee Station.—A fine of 10s, and costs or 14 days was impoied.

Locomoter ataxy is regarded by the medical profes- sion as the most severe and the most hopeless form of paralysis, more especially when it developea slowly from an injury to the brain or Epinal colum, as in the case of Mr. George Greenwood, which was certainly in- curable by ordinary medicine. That he was definitely cured by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills is one more evidence of the fact that they are not like ordinary medicine, and that they cure when urdinary medicine fails. Mr. Greenwood is a clerk employed in the offices of the L. and N.W. Railway. He lives at 17 Holt's Terrace Longsight, Manchester, and his cure—a case (says the " Stockport Advertieer ") that would have been beyond belief had it not been for the testimony of unimpeach- able witnesses —is impressive and instructive. "About eighteen months ago," be said, " I sought medical advice. I suffered most excruciating pains which flew about to different parts of the body, sometimes in one part, sometimes in another. I practically lost the use of my limbs, and got so that I could not go out alone. When I walked, I stag- . Rered from side to side like a drunken man. I dared not come down or go up- _ 5.7 stairs alone, and when I had put n•-• 2 out the gas, I would be unable to stand, so - powerless was I to control my limbs in the dark. The doctors soon diagnosed my complaint ; they told me I was suf-

"LOST um or iax LIMBS." feting from loco- motor ataxy, and they gave me not the faintest hope of recovery. I went to Liverpool, to a hospital there, and the doctor told me I must never go outside after dark."

"And were you working all this time 2" asked the reporter. " Oh, no, indeed. I could grasp nothing of less di- mensions than the handle of a•good stout walking-stick, and to hold a pen was an impossibility. I was away ten months." _

" And what did you da "I heard of Dr. Williams' P nk Pills, and determined to try them, which I did, with marvellous results. The doctor at Liverpool had told me I should never Tx alk again without a stick." " And now?" .
" Now Ige to work every morning at five o'clock, and have being doing for months—and I never take a stick."

"And would you describe yourself as cured 2" "Yes. I used to be so bad at night that I coulrnt lie in bed. Many a time I have crawled downstairs and lit the fire, preferring to sit here in this chair to en- during the miseries and pain and sleeplessness in bed."

MORLCAMBE v. RUNCORN.

Tnis return Lancashire League match w-as played at Morecambe in good weather on Saturday. About 200 were present when Farmer started against a very strong wind. In the early stages Morecambe made the best of the wind. Houghton and Sefton next had to save very quickly. Blacow was smart in getting the ball out, but the game progressed very slowly. The enthusiasm of the spectators was raised when Elkin had a free kick in a favourable positic n, but it failed, and Runcorn got to midfield. Butterworth put a fine kick-out, Hadwin returning hack to Houghton who, having a stiff wind to face, could not make headway. Houghton was damaged in a tackle and the game stopped a while. Score at halftime—Runcorn 0, Morecambe 0. The second half was also very even, and the game ended a pointless draw.

ST. HELENS RECS v. WIDNES. These teama met in a friendly fixture at St. Helens on Saturday before one thousand spectators. Both teams were fully represented. The Recs. started before a strong wind, the ball going into touch. Sime effective kicking by the visitors transferred hostilities to neutral ground, where a series of scrimmages ensued. Some grand pss3lng by Crossley and Archer cham;ed the venue to the Widnes half, play being of a scrambling character. A free kick taken by Pennington enabled the Recs. to reach the Widnes line. Rispan was conspicuous with a grand run, the ball being knocked on from a rush. Hughes, v.ith a judicious kick, averted the danger. Sub- sequeatly end-to-end play followed, each side attacking in turn. From a rush to the Recreation half Peters scored. Brennan failing to vipmt. A moment later Murphy intercepted and scored an uniMptoved try. Half-time—Widnes 0-2-0, Rezreatlon, nil. Final—Widnes 2 tries, St, Helens Recs nil.

WaaaiNcixoN A v. STOCKPORT A.—There would be an attendance of about 4,000 spectators at this match on the Wilclerspool Enclosure on Saturday. This increased number was probably due to the announcement that Barber and Broady would be seen together in the three- quarter line. Barber, however, did not turn oat, and when the teams faced each other, they were composed as follows :—Warrineton : Boscow, full back; Broady, Lawless, Cross, and Carey. thre,-quarter backs ; Scott and Bate, half backs ; Andrews,Eden,Royle,Hatton nineham,Knight, Jolley, and Timmins.forwards. Stock- port : Simister, full back ; Grange, Chorlton, Gidlow, and Vernon, Vernon, three-quarter backs ; Norris and McLough' lin, half backs ; Hildebrand, Gibson, Mottershead- Shuffiebotham, King, Hall worth, Goodall, and Daven- port, forwards. At the commencement of hostilities. Cross was absent, and thus weakened, the home team had tho worst of the opening play. The ball was carried over the home goal line, and Broady just suc- ceeded in preventing a score by kicking dead. On Cross making his appearance, a different complexion was Placed on the game, and Warrington had a spell of pass- kW.. Cross was given a pass near the line but failed to hold the ball, and the opportunity was lost. Lawless and Carey also made poor use of openings, and despite the fact that Warrington were favoured with the wind, they were unable to score, and on changing ends there was a blank score sheet. On resuming Broady was early prominent by a speedy run, but he was pulled down by Simistor. The Warrington forwards heeled out F' plead idly, and gave the backs plenty to do, but many chances went a begging. Scott almost got Over the coveted line, but the Stockport backs who were playing a much smarter game transferred play to the Warring- ton end. A neat passing movement being taken part in by Sate, Scott, Carey, Cross, and Boyle almost ended in disaster for the visitors, but they succeeded in keeping their lines intact. Boscow, by erratic play, enabled the visitors to get into the Warrington 25, and Chorlton get- ting a goad opportunity dropped a srlendid goal. The home team strove hard to gain something tangible, but failed, and retired beaten by one dropped goal (2 points) to nil.

div.head: TRAP ACCIDENT.
div.p: TRAP ACCIDENT.

On Saturday afternoon,Mr. Joseph Potter,farmer, Culcheth, was driving a horse and trap along Irlam- street when, the animal stumbling, Mr. Potter was thrown ont of the trap. Inspector Philips, Detec- tive Williamson, and P.C. Barnett ran out from the Police Station and found Mr. Potter lying in front of the trap wheel. They carried him into the sta- tion, where he rested for a while,and was then able to proceed home, having sustained no injury be- yond a slight cut on the cheek.

RUNCORN HORNETS V.RUNCORN RECS. l'A" TESM.--Tha Hornets kicked off.a good return being made. Play was was in the hem@ 25 for some time. The visitors often , kicked dead from centre of field, whilst the wing for- wards stopped the home team from pasoing. The Hornet by a passing movement were soon at the other end,but a flying kick brought play back. Score at half time :—Hornets nil, Rees nil. Playing with the wind the home team pressed and an appeal for off-side being allowed Joyce missed from an easy position. Play was soon back again, and from a good dribble G. Higgins scored under the post. Dean kicked a goal, which was followed by a penalty by Dean soon afterwards. S. Hughes was the next to score after a tricky run. The kick at goal failed. A miserable game ended in a win for Hornets by 10 points to nil. WOOLSTON v. Caorr.—About 400 assembled on the ground of the first named team to witness this return match. More than ordinary interest was centered in the meeting, and the rivalry which exists between these neighbouring teams was manifested during the progress of the match, for the excitement was keen throughout. The first match had resulted in a victory for Croft. Per Saturday's match Woolston bad strengthened their team. The opening phases went directly in favour of the home men,whose forwards worked the scrimmage in clever atria, and afforded their backs rare opportuni- ties for maintaining the attack. A brilliant run by Smith received but little support, and though the Croftonians were kept on the defensive they kept their lines Intact, and at the interval there was no score. Wooloton had again the best of it on resuming, and the forwards de- monstrated their snaartness in a marked manner. Even- tually Trigger followed up a kick, and Taylor being in difficulties, the former charged the return and scored,the try not being improved. The fast pace which had characterized the game throughout was maintained until the chwourd though Croft pressed occasionally the back play of Woolston remained sound, and the interesting match ended in favour of the home side by a try to nil. Afterwards the teams sat down to a capital repast at the .#ope and Anchor, provided by Host Daintith.
ASSOCIATION. EDELSTEN ATHLETIC V. SANKEY WESLEYANS.—ThiS match was played on the Wesleyan ground,and resulted in an easy win for Edelsten by five goals to nil.

WARRINGTON WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. Owing to the difficulties which he arisen .F.l previous years it was found advisable to limit the number of tickets for the soiree and ball in connec- tion with the Warrington Women's Liberal Associa, tion, held in the Parr Hall, on Thursday last week. Consequently the attendance was not so large as on former occasions, but nevertheless the ball, was a success in every respect. The hall had again been elaborately decorated by Messrs. Hesketh and Dutton with their usual good taste. Dancing commenced about 8 o'clock, and was continued un- til nearly three. There would be about 350 persons present. Mr. Arthur Browne made an ideal M.C., and ho was assiste.l in his duties by the follow- ing stewards :—Mr. C. J. Holmes, Councillor D. Tinnion, Mr. George E. Clay. Mr. W. Bibby. Mr. J. E. Warren, Mr. R. Woods, Mr. W. .Mounfield,and Mr,Jarnes Critchley,the indefatigable hon. secretary to the Ball Committee. Mr. A. H. Crosfield favoured the ball with his presence, and it may be added that be presented a large quantity of flowers which had been sent from Cannes. These were placed in the ladies' cloakroom for the use of the ladies. Mr. R. H. Pearson's band was in atten- dance, and added much to the success of the gathering. Twenty - two dances were gone through, the following being the programme : Polka, "Rum Turn Pam'; waltz, "La Frivolle" Lancers, "Goisha";waltz,"Germania"; pas de quatre, "Knickerbocker"; lancers, "French Maid"; waltz "Cinder Ellen's Dream"; lancers, "Haddon Hall"; pas de qoatre, "Canadian"; waltz, "Sur La Plage"; lancers, "The Yashmak"; schottische, "Modesta"; lancers, "Circus Girl"; waltz, "Sweet Eventide"; pas de quatre. SAD FATALITY TO A WATERCRESS GATHERER.-.-MT. J. C. Bate, coroner, held an inquest on Tuesday, at the Frodsham Police Court, on the body of Jane Faulkner, aged 37 years, of Marsh Green, Frodsham Lordship, who accidentally fell into a ditch on Saturday and was drowned.—John Henry Faulkner said deceased was his aunt, and in consequence of what was said to him about 12.45 on Saturday, he went to Bickerstaffe's Marsh, and there found deceased lyingface downwards in the water. He pulled her out but she was dead.—Susan Ainsworth stated that she had breakfast with deceased on Saturday morning at ten o'clock. She appeared in her usual health and spirits, and about ten rninut6s to twelve she asksd witness to lend her a rake to get some watercress. She took witness's little boy with her and in a while after the lad came back saying that Mrs. Faulkner had fallen in the ditch.—Sergeant Clays said he saw deceased on the side of the ditch. Her mouth, eyes, and nostrils, were full of mud. In her pockets was a pulse and 14s. 9d., lin cash. He was of opinion that deceased accidentally fell into Vie ditch and was suffocated. There was only four or five inches of water in the ditch. There was a lot of mud.--The jury returned a verdict that deceased was " Acchdently suffocated." THREATENING A SCHOOL-MISTRES9.—At the Frodsham Police Court on Tuesday before Messrs. C. Reynolds and A. Thomas, Mary Ellen Ball was summoned fcr using threats towards Mary Roberts, school-mistress at Church- t. National school on Ole 24th December. Miss Roberts stated that defendant came to school and complained about her correcting one of her children. She threatened to pull witness out of the school, and make her as she would not know herself. Defendant said complainant had abuse 4 one of her children. She was fined the costs 12s. fit and was bound over to keep the peace. DRUNIC AND DISORDERLY.—At .the same court on the earns day,William Nickson, was charged on a warrant in being drunk and disorderly on the 9th December. Ser- geant Clays proved the case and defendant was fined ss. and 17s. 93. costs. I Oa Wednesday before Mr. J. Olkleston, Arthur Jones, a tramp was committed to prison for seven days with hard labour for begging the previous day at Helsby. -

PENKETIL
RETURN BILLIARD MATCH.

On Saturday the team of billiard players from the Runcorn Liberal Club came to Penketh to play the re- turn match. The match at Runcorn was a most enjoy- able affair, and the Penketh members determined to spare no efforts to give the Runcorn men ars appropri- ate return for their hospitality. The Runcorn men arrived early in the afternoon and at once commenced to play. At six o'clock, the whole party adj:urned to the Wesleyan school where a sumptuous tea had been prepared by Mesdames Mainley and White, assisted by Miss H. M. Mainley, E. Barlow, and C. Wilkinson. After tea, a vote of thanks was accorded by acclamation to the ladies for their efforts on the players' behalf. Mrs. Mainley responded, and the party returned to the Club where the remainder of the games were played. On the occasion of the first match the Runcorn team won by 192 points, but on Saturday at the conclusion the Pen- keth team were 100 points to the good on their table. Messrs. J. Lewis (president, Penketh L.C.) and Mr. H. Wright, the captain of the Runcorn team, both ex- pressed the great pleasure the meeting had given, it having proved an unqualified success.
