LIBERAI: Ciina.—On Friday last weei the fioneert pro- moted by the officials of the Penketh Liberal Club was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom. In former years a combined tea party and concert had been held, but this year it was resolved to leave out the tea, and provide a really good concert for the patrons. An extrem, ly strong programme was arranged, the committee having gone to great trouble and expense to secure the artistes. Much disappointment was evidenced by the large audi- ence, on the chairman (Mr. C. E. Parker) reading a tele- gram from the well-known humorist, Mr. J. McDermott of Liverpool. stating his inability to be present. He, however, had in some part compensated for his abseLce, by sending a substitute, Mr. J. R. Daryl. The pro- gramme was opened by Miss Nolland and Mr. Tom Boothroyd with a mandoline duett, March "Empres4," which was greatly appreciated. Mr. Arthur Griffiths r was heard to advantage in "Our Jack," and later in "Come into the garden Maud." Miss Hilda Garnett was well received in her two songs " The Castilian Maid," and "Awake." Mr. W. Podmore's flute solos were well deserving of the applause they produced, being " Robin Adair" and "The Pilgrim of Love." Miss Jessie Edwards, of Liverpool, possesses a very sweet and telling seprano voice, and her rendering of " Swallows," and " Sing sweet Bird," was received with unstinted applause, a recall being demanded. The two well known bass solos " The mighty deep," and "Out on the deep" were un- dertaken by Mr. Harold Fleslop of Liverpool, who is one of the best bass singers heard for some time in this vil- lage, the audience testifying their approval in no nig- gardly manner. Mr. Tom Bouthroyd was also to the fore with two excellently rendered violin solos a selec- tion from "Faust," and "Valse de Concert." Mr. J. R. Daryl, as the humourist, appeared three times, and his efforts met with great success. He is extremely clever on the pianoforte, his burlesque on "Paderewski" being very smart and funny. "A Tour round the world in two hours" was also a very clever piece of work,and was much appreciated. Mrs. C. E. Parker accompanied the artistes on the pianoforte.

THE DREDGING OF THE RIVER,

A circular has been issued by the owners of land on the banks of the Mersey near Warrington, 're- minding them that under the agreement between the Corporation and the Manchester Ship Canal Company, the company are bound to dredge not only in front of any existing wharves, but also in front of any future wharves constructed within five years from the 9th April, 1896. After that period the dredging will only be done by the com- pany in front of new wharves at the expense of the owners of such wharves. WARRINGTON TEMPERA NCB FEDERATION.

7TIIE WARRINGTON ART AND INDUS:
T RIA L EXHIBITION.
PREPARATIONS IN PROGRESS.

The art and industrial exhibition decided upon last year by the Corporation, but which has from time to time been postponed owing to various causes,is to be opened on March 30th,and will be con- tinued until April 12th. Mr. W.J.Hooper has under- taken to manage the whole of the arrangements,and the exhibition will be held in the Parr Hall under the patronage of the Town Council and the Cham- ber of Commerce. The whole of the liabilities will be met by the contractor, who has rented the Hall from the Corporatiou.A plan of the building for the exhibition has been prenared. It is intended to use the small hall or vestibule for machinery in motion, and the large hall for tr ide exhibits. Art treasures and other exhibits will be displayed in the ante rooms and the different'entrances. There'will only be one ntrance eto the exhibition, and that the one niarest the gallery steps . The number of app ications by tradesmen and manufacturers for space—which has been fixed at Is. 61. per sq. foot—is sufficient to cover all that is available. Priority of choice of position will be gi.eu to local exhibitors There is every likeli- hood of the exhibition being representative of the varied industries of the town, and under the direc- tion of Mr. Hooper,who has had a large experience in exhibitions of this kind, it should prove a suc- cess. At intervals each day a musical entertainment will be given by a celebrated ladies' orchestra which has been specially engaged from London. Cookery demonstrations and other attractions will be provided. The exhibition will open at one o'clock ch day and continue open until ten o'clock.

HOME OFFICE JTJSTICE.

Sir,—lt appears that Mr. Wallace Spriggs, the young I man who was, in November last,sentenced by Mr. Justice tirantham to five years' penal servitude for an assault upon a young lady cyclist in North Wales,has been only liberated on a license, but excused from reporting him- self as persons released on license usually are. This is a wretched half measure at hnt. There ought to be a free pardon, with compensation; but I suppose the Home Secretary wanted to let the Judge down easy. The decision in the Pena,'h intimidation case seems to be still weaker. The acq i.ttal of tise constable only proves that there as a Tease., hie doubt as to whether he committed perjury. Ti .4 left room for a reasonable doubt as to his guilt. Bac, the Home Secretary was satisfied that the constable swore the truth, wny did he reduce the sentence—passed by his brother ? The case of Mr. Spriggs affords a good argument against the latest flogging move on the part of the great unpaid. If these persons had their way, Mr.Spriggs (as well as Pot- ter and the Rev. Mr. Hatch,two almost forgotten cases) would have been flogged,to say nothing of Colonel Valen- tine Baker. I beg leave to ask all who are opposed to the further extension of flogging in our penal system to join the Prison Reform Department of the Humanitar- ian League, which will use its best efforts on the other side.—Yours, JOSEPH COLLINSON, Honorary Secretary. Humanitarian League Office, 53, Chancery-Lthe, London.

div.head: SUNDAY OBSERVANCE.
div.p: SUNDAY OBSERVANCE.

Sir,—lt isnot a matter of surprise to me that "lons " bas not the ability to grasp the bearing of the passages I cited in my last, seeing he has so palpably shown in this correspondence his want of familiarity with the Bible ; and had it not been for the disingenuous manner in which he again introduces the desirability of resting from labour, I should perhaps not have troubled you with another communication. I suppose most people are agreed that men and animals are better for periodical times of rest, but this does not prove that it is comman- ded by God. We do not dispute nor have WR disputed that God gave the" Maslen Law "of which the fourth Commandment is only a portion; but we do assert most empathically that that Law—the Mosaic—is ended, and we further assert that it is utterly impossible for the enactments of that Law to be now fulfilled as any one may readily see by referring to its numerous items. With regard to that position touching on Sabbath Observance, we may remark further that if it were now operative there would of necessity have to be a change in the day observed as a day of rest, for the command was respecting our Saturday, not our Sunday. I a man were told by his employer in plain language i.) go to Manchester, and instead of go- ing to that town he went to Liverpool because others were going there,he would be acting quite as reasonably as does the man who regards Sunday observance as now necessary because Saturday was some time ago com- manded to be observed as a holy day. There is abso- lutely no scriptural authority for observing Sunday more than any other day. Though the disciples met en the Sunday for breaking of bread, that does not prove anything, and seeing that Christ reiterated only nine of the commandments and that we have the assurance in the scriptures that Be is the end of the law, we accept that assurance,even though we should then be in opposi- tion to the sects " lona " names. If " lona " will only carefully and without prejudice examine the Bible ho may possibly find there is no authority for many of the beliefs held by the various sects.—Yours truly, R. G. L.

div.head: MESSRS. PETER WALKER AND SONS AND THEIR TENANTS.
div.p: MESSRS. PETER WALKER AND SONS AND THEIR TENANTS.
A CREWE HOTEL CLOSED.

At the Crewe Borough Sessions on Tuesday, Mr. T. Latham, on behalf of Mr. A. Tweedale, applied to the Bench to grant a espy of a license held by William Byers in respect of the George and Dragon Hotel, Mill- street, one of the houses of Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, and also a transfer of the license from the said William Byers to Albert Tweedale. Mr. H. J. Williams objected to both applications on behalf of the present rcence holder, Byers. The case created a great deal of ' oterest, and the hearing occupied a considerable time. The facts were these. Byers was for some time a manager of the George and Dragon for Messrs. Walker, and when the Crewe magistrates insisted upon Messrs. Walker replacing their managers in Crewe with tenants he was accepted as a tenant, and continued to conduct the house. Be paid Messrs. Walker £95 for the stock and utensils under the fresh arrangement. The agree- ment between the tenant and the firm was produced at the time of the change (about four years ago), and at the request of the Bench it was endorsed with the prices which the tenant should pay to the firm for liquors. In October last Byers applied to the firm for a cheaper class of beer than he had heretofore been getting, but it was a class of beer which was priced on his agree- ment. He saw Mr. Peter Wright, the manager for Messrs. Walker, at Liverpool, and Mr. Wright told him that it was a condition with the Crewe tenants that only the best quality of beer should be sold at their houses, and that if he were not satisfied he could give three months' notice. Byers had before this asked for a cheaper beer, and as Messrs. Walker still sent the higher quality he returned three of the barrels and pur- chased beer elsewhere. After the interview with Mr. Wright in Liverpool he returned home and found that during his absence Messrs. Walker had sent to Crewe and served a notice to quit on his wife. The notice to quit expired about a week ago. Mr.Bilsborrow, one cf Messrs. Walker's agents, came over to Crewe, took stock, paid Byers some £5O or £6O for stock and uten- sils, and Byers gave him possession of the house. He, however, still retained the license, arid claimed £2OO for " the great personal labour, expense, and work he bad done in increasing the trade of the house since he became the tenant," The house has been closed ever since. Mr. Bilsborrow. a representative of Messrs. Walker, said that he paid Byers £5O or £6O when lee gave up the house. He still withheld the license. He aware that Byers was claiming £2OO from Messrs. Wa'ker for an alleged breach of the covenants of his agreement. Mr. Peter Wright was next called. Be said that when Byers was accepted as tenant of the house he was told that the firm would only supply these houses with ales of the highest quality. When Byers was a rnana,mr for the firm they were thoroughly satisfied with him, so much so that they continued him as their tenant. He admitted that the agreement bore a list of prices of cheap beers, but there were three classes of cheaper beer which they did not supply to their tenants. Mr. Byers had not asked for the cheaper beer until recently. He only applied for it when he was free of debt ti the firm. The firm had allowed him nearly ten years to nay the £95 for stock and utensils when he became the tenant, The Chairman said that when these agreements were produced to the Bench Mesers.Walker endorsed on them a list of prices, come of which they never intended their tenants to have the advantage of. They had thus broken their own agreement. The Bench understood that these agreements were bona-fide on both sides, their idea be- ing that tenants slaould be supplied at fair trade prices, and so get a living without having to resort to any ex- troardinary or untrual effort, which might injure the tenant and damage the firm. Mr.Latham : 'More was no object whatever in putting these prices in the agreement. Byers knew at the time that those prices were not intended for him. They charged Byers with " wilfully withholding "the license. Mr. Wright was cross-examined as to the meaning of the " long pull," and he said the firm did not recognise the term. But their manager gave liberal measure. Re thought the term " long pull" was an obnoxious term. The Chairman maid lie had seen in one public-house window in Crewe "Long pull given here." Mr. Wright : We give liberal measure. Mr. Williams : When a person goes into one of your houses and asks for half a piat of beer, he get's a pint ? Mr. Wright : I think the question is very stupid. But does he ? Does be get three half-pints for 20. ? I do not know what measure is given. They give liberal measure. The sole reason you gave Byers notice to quit was be- cause he asked to be supplied with ale at 3s. a barrel, according to the list on his agreement ?—The reason we gave Byers notice was that he was offensive, and that he demanded the cheaper beer. Mr. Williams said that Measrs. Walker had deceived the Bench by producing an agreement containing prices whico was never intended to be acted up to in their dealings with their tenants. William Byers was called. He said he held the license because be thought he had a legal claim on the firm for , not acting up to their agreement. He could not afford I to retail ale which cost him 48s. a barrel to outside cus- tomers. The custom at Messrs. Walker's houses was to give three half-pints to the pint, and to do that with als which cost him forty-eight shillings a barrel left him no profit. He understood that other tenants were getting better terms than he. He WAS selling three barrels a week at a loss. He wrote asking for a cheaper ale for the outside trade, but the firm refused to supply it, and when he complained personally he got his notice. After a great deal of evidence, the magistrates retired. On their return the Chairman said: We have given a somewhat extended and very careful consideration to this case, and the following is our decision :—The magis- trates are not satisfied, from the evidence submitted to them, that the license is withheld without any legal right to withhold the came. Thee' therefore refuse to grant the application for a certificated copy of the license. The decision of the Bench means, therefore, that, although the firm have posseesion of the house, the late tenant retains the license, so that for the present the house remains closed. The house is one of the largest in the borough, and is situated in one of the principal main streets to the meation.

div.head: RUNCORN'S WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: RUNCORN'S WATER SUPPLY.
REPORT OF THE MEDICAL OFFICER.

At the monthly meeting of the Urban District Ceuncil on Thursday, held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, Mr. J. W. Lightburn presiding, the Health Com- mittee reported that having received a letter from the Local Government calling attention to the subject of the water supply of the district, and to the importance of the wholesomeness of the supply of water in view of the serious epidemics of enteric fever which have of recent years been brought about by specific contamination of water supplies in different parts of the country ; and having also received an analysts of the water made by Professor Boyce, of Liverpool University, at the re- quest of the Water Committee, they asked the Medical Officer of Health to report as to the wholesomeness and freedom from contamination of the water supplied by the Water Department. The report—a rather lengthy document—was printed in the minutes. In the course of it Dr. McDougall said that at the present time the water supply is absolutely free from sewage pollution and from speeific disease pro- ducing germs, as testified to by the ample bacterio- logical examination of Professor Boyce, and subse- quently confirmed by the recent analysis of Mr. Carter Bell, the county analyst. The report of Professor Boyce contained the words •'Comparable to the average sample of tap water. No evidence of sewage contamination." In reply to a question by the committee as to whether there is anything in the water detrimental to health,Dr. McDougall replied as follows in a letter :—" lam not prepared to say what effect excess of chlorides in drinking water may have on individual constitution. My views as to its suitability for a town supply is al- ready embodied in my report." Dr. Carter Bell reported " As regards the Organic Matter, this is first class water, but it contains too much salt, therefore it makes the water unsuitable for a town supply." Mr. T. Dean said that in complianee with the wish of the Council the Health Committee went into the question el the water supply. From the analyees procured the committee considered they had done their duty inasmuch as they proved that there was no sewage contamina- tion. Of course there was an excess of salt in the water but with that, he took it,the committee had nothing to do with, as it was a matter for the Water Committee. They were perfectly certain that there was no contamin- ation detrimental to he dth. He proposed the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. W. Collier seconded. He thought Dr. McDougall's report very unsatisfactory. He (Dr. McDougall)wae asked by the Health Committee whether there was anything in the water detrimental to healca. He replied th it he was not prepared to say. He considered that their medical officer of health should give them an answer to a simple question and they ought to understand and have his candid opinion as to whether he was to be their friend or to be against them. —Mr. Imison inquired whether an appendix in the re- port referred to water which had been taken from the towr's supply and analysed, or whether it referred to water from a private well.Mr.Handley: It is farm water. It is water from a private well.—Mr. Imison, continuing said then it was most unfair. It being a water from a private well it was distinctly unfair to suggest that there was any necessicy for appendix D.being referred to at all. Mr.Pritchard said the question first came before them ! owing to their having received a circular from the Local Government Board pointing out the necessity of having a wholesome supply of water, and also because of the ,1 recent epidemics which had been brought about by I specific contamination. What they had to consider WAS "have we a complete answer to the letter addressed to us." What bearing had analyses taken five or six years age, on the question ? They had a complete answer to the circular in 'the two last analyses of Dr. Carter Bell and Professor Boyce, upon the specific question of con- tamination which the Local Gavernment Board raised as eegarded the organic matter. The former gentleman replied" This is a first-class water," and Mr. Boyce re- plied "comparable to the average sample of tap water. No evidence of sewage contamination." Their Officer stated that " at present the water supply is absolutely free from sewage pollution, and from specific disease producing germs, as testi fled to by the ample analyses of these two gentlemen." He considered that that was a complete answer to the circular of the Local Government Board. He considered and he thought every other reasonable man would think that their water was free from contamination.— Mr. Imison said he thoroughly agreed with the general tone of Mr. Pritchard's remarks, but disagreed with the strong tone of Mr. Collier's. What did he want the medical officer to be ? Did he want him to he a mere creature to register the wishes of that Council ? He was the guardian of the public health. He (the speaker) was sure that the public would prefer that the Dr. should act in the guarded manner he had done in this matter rather than to act as a mere machine. He agreed with Mr. Pritchard that they had a complete and satisfactory re- ply from the doctor, a reply which he considered was re- quired for the purpose of sending t e the Local Govern- ment Board. They were told that there was no sewage contamination and also that there was no case of typhoid fever traceable to the drinking of the water. What in ore could they wish for. The doctor's suggestion that they should have more frequent analyses was a very good ' one to insure the possibility of detecting any sewage contamination. They ought to reassure the public that every proper course was being taken and whatever little anxiety was aroused in the public mind would be allayed.—Mr. Speakman said he was very glad that they I had reassuring reports from Dr. McDougall and Dr. Bell. He thought the subject was prematurely raised at the last Council meeting and it caused a tremendous storm in a tea pot. 1 He was perfectly satisfied that the water was really fit to partake of and that there was no fear about it.—Mr. Kirkham inquired what chlorides were in the water when they took the works over. In his lest analysis Dr. Bell said there was 41;1—Mr. Handley said there were 23. when they took the works over. He took it from D. last anelysis that there wee no lime salt in the water, although there were 41 grains per gallon in the water of chlorine and chloridee, will there was no phos- phoric acid. Chlorides c3nsiated of two things, elm- mon salt or animal salt. In all animal sewage there was animal salt and they were distinctly dangersus because they pointed to sewage pollution. If they read Dr. Bell's analysis they would find that there was no ammonia, and thus proving their Medical Officer's statement that there was no sewage contamination whatever. He agreed with Mr.lmison in reference to having frequent analyses of their water. He did not think when he raised the question at the last meeting that the thing was prema- ture. When he heard that a man would not drink any- more of Runcorn water and when they heard that manu- facturers went to other towns for it, he thought it was quite time to raise the question. But they would now feel that they had is good supply. The fact of the water being salty made it bard. Runcorn water was always hard.—Other members spoke and the minutes were after wards confirmed. . ,

Gill3spie, William Lloyd, a collier living in Robin's Row, Newton, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Earlestown on Satur- day night and was fined 53. an I costa. PRIDE OF EARLESToWN TEMPLE, This Temple held its usual weekly meeting in the Co-operative Hall,presided over by Bro. J. Sin- gleton, lodge chaplain. There was a large attend- ance of members and friends, Bro. J. Woods being invited to give an address on the "Font Fold Pledge," which was listened to with interest by the children,

div.p: VULCAN WESLEYAN Caesnt.

On Sunday the opening of the new organ in the above chapel was celebrated by two sermons preached afternoon and evening by the Rev. D. Jones, superintendent minister. There were good congregations, and special hymns were sung by the choir. Collections were made in aid of the organ fund.

div.head: P.S.A.
div.p: P.S.A.

At the usual weekly meeting on Sunday after- noon there was a good attendance. Mr It Thompson presided, and the principal speaker was Mr. Capon. A recital was given by Miss ft Warburton, and vocal selections were submitted by Mr Oldham,and Mr A E Howarth presided at the piano.
_ THE CHURCH ASSOCIATION VAN AT EARLBS- TOWN.

On Sunday evening --M; -bourtney delivered an address to a large number of people on the Earles- town Market Ground. At the close of his discourse he said that his visit to Earlestown was drawing to a close, but before leaving he wished to compliment the Earlestown police force, for the excelleni arrangements they had made for his protection and for the satisfactory manner in which those arrange- ments had been carried out. he said the Earles- town people ought to be proud that they had such a staff of men amongst them.

div.head: TRH MUSICAL FESTIVAL Al EARLESTOWN.
div.p: TRH MUSICAL FESTIVAL Al EARLESTOWN.

In connection with the above the Rev. T. R. Matthews invited all those who composed the chorus to a social evening at the Mission Hall on Tuesday evening. Almost all of those who took part availed themselves of the invitation,and a very pleasant time was passed. Tea was provided, and afterwards games and dancing were indulged in, several of the party contributing songs. It was announced that the finanLial result of the festival had been eminently satisfactory, and that there would be a surplus after completing the work on the organ.

div.head: SINGULAR ACCIDENT TO A BOY.
div.p: SINGULAR ACCIDENT TO A BOY.

Oa Satu-r-da-y-idt-e-rn-o-o-r-i-a-li-o-y r-iam-ed-A-r-din, living with his parents in Lower Legh-street, Earlestown, met with a singular accident by which he sustained a broken thigh. The boy, who is about 7 years of age, was stood watching some youths play football, when the ball rolled near him and in attempting to kick it, he fell and was unable to rise. He was carri3d into the house and afterwards to the surgery of Dr. Mouncey, when it was found that he had sustained a fracture of the thigh. The injured limb was set, and the lad is progressing as well as can be expected. THEFT BY COLLIER. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wed- nesday, Michael Belly, collier, Earlestown, was charged with stalling a shawl value 63. from Mr. Jones's pawnshop between the 18th and 19th Jan. —Mark Coyne,assistant to Mr. Jones,Market-street, Earlestown,said the shawl was safe at 4 p.m on the 18th January and missing at 6.30 p.m. Witness found it pledged at Mr. Pritchard's pawnshop for 33.—Margaret Inglish,prisoner's landlady,deposed to Dawning the shawl at the request of the prisoner. She knew nothing about tee shawl.—Mr. H. E. Pritchard deposed to giving last witness 33. on the shawl, and then receiving inquiries about it from Mr. Coyne.—P.C. Clarke said he apprehended pri- soner in Crow-lane on Tuesday night,and in answer t, the charge he said another man gave him the shawl. They could not find the other man.—The magistrates bound prisoner over to come up for judgment when called upon, and pay costs.

For the first offence prisoner would be fined 55. and costs; for the assault on the police, 10s. and costs ; and in the case of Mr. Hayes he would be bound over fer six months in two sureties, himself in £1.13 and his father in £5.

In the South Wolverhampton division,which has never before been polled, the Liberal Unionist candidate, Mr. J. L. Gibbons, was returned on 'l'hursday by 4,115 votes against 4,004 recorded for the Liberal candidate, Mr. G. B. Thorne. Mr. Gibbons, who had therefore a majority of 111, succeeds to the sea: tor so many years occupie4 by the late Mr. Villiers.

div.p: HE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 4, 1898 NOTES BY THE WAY AT EA RIESTOWN.

(BY AN OCCASIONAL COBABSPONDENT.) The last day upon which application for tickets can be made for the 014 Folks Treat, is Saturday next,the social gathering taking place on Thursday evening next. Everything is being done to make the affair a success, and it is hoped the old people will carry away with them pleasant memories of the event.

Mr. Courtney the propagandist of the National Protestant League drew a favourable contrast be- tween the police of Golborne, and of Earlestown on Sunday night,and well he nrght. During his short stay at Go!borne, he was roughly used, and accord- ing to report, he did not receive adequate protec- tion from the Gnlborne police. When be came to Earlestown, the case was altogether different, and a strong force of police took care that he pursued his avocation without molestation.

-- The musical festival which was given in St. John's Church, last week, was of a very successful nature in every way. Mr. Radford deserves every praise for the excellence of the performance which he certainly contributed to in no small measure. The soloists were excellent, and the choir was as evenly balanced as it was possible to get it. I think Mr. Radford might do worse than repeat the experiment on some future occasion.

WARRINGTON OUTPLAYED AT STOCKPORT. The Warrington team bad a Cheshire engagement on Saturday, Stockport being their opponents.Barly in the Season Stockport were handsomely defeated n the Wilderspool enclosure, but they amply atoned for this ignominy on ,Faturday by rubbing in a score of 2 goals, 3 tries to a try. Warrington • took a week team away—the lack of capable re- serves again showing itself—while the Cheshire men had a better representation than they have had for some time. Saville was sufficiently re- covered to turn out after eleven weeks absence. Boscow was absent from the home side, Heesom filling the vacancy, while Morrison was given a trial next to Hallam on the threequarter line. An- other fine afternoon favoured the game, though the wind was too strong for good play. There were about .3,00 Q spectators assembled, and the referee was Mr. J. Skidmore, Broughton Rangers. The teams were as folle,we ; Stockport : Hoggartle, full back; Robinson, Worsley, Sands, and Saville, threequarters; Allen and Clarke, half-backs; Moss, Burrows, Brooke, Sharpe, Hague, Davidson, Garside, and Hampson, forwards. Warrington :—lleesom, full back; Moores, Isherwood, Hallam and Morrison, three-quarters; Bate and Duck- worth, half backs; Taylor, Deakin, Naylor, Barrett, Hill, Swift, Mason, and Robey, forwards. Stockport won the toss and took up a position with the wind behind. Taylor kicked off for Warrington, ' Robinson responding with a quick run to centre. Bate soon got possession, but his pass was snapped up by SI, ville, whom Moores quickly grassed. A fine effort by the Warrington forwards endangered the home line,Hog- garth only just securing the oval in the corner. Allen was penalised and Mason made a good,but uncessful at- tempt at goal from the touch has. Play was transferred to the opposite side,where Duckworth smartly got away and gave Morrison a nice pass on the line which was missed. Alien and Rebinsen transferrad play to centre and the latter put in a cross-kick which Isherwood re- turned smartly. Stockport entered the borne half and Allen started a clever passing movement which reached Robinson who sprinted down the touch line unti Heesom stepped in the way. Up to this time there had been little to choose between the teams but Stockport's superior back play began to tell. After Worsley had only just failed at goal from a penalty. Sands punted high and the home forwards crossed the Warrington line, fleenom touching down in the nick of time. Isherwo d dribbled clevery to the centre, where play seemed safe for Warrington.l Allen,ho wever,handed to VI orsley, who tricked Hallam and passed to Robinson who sprinted nearly behind the Warrington goal before touching down. Saville failed at goal. Stockport re- turned Warrington's drop-out and Isherwood misjudging the ball near the line gave a soft try to Davidson, Saville this' time adding the goal. This was unexpected on both sides, and fairly staggered Warringtou. Bate, Hallam and Morrison exchanged but the latter made little headway. flozgarth got penalised for obstruation on his own line,but Sands punted out,Morrison promptly falling on tbe ball. Saville again took Bate's pass, but Moores sent him in touch. Several oaseing movements by Warrington were crude and ineffective, though the two half backs made eeod openings. Clarke made a good drop at goal when in the visitors' half, and Robinson had a fine chance spoiled through a forward past. Chiefly by strong forward play Warring ton returned hotly to the attack, Hallam failing at an- other penalty kick. Stockport were hard pressed when Bate got the ball out and giving Duckworth a smart pass, the latter scored a clever try in the corner. Tay- lor missed the goal by very little. Bate and Barrett kept play on the home line, but Stockport got clear by kick- ing with the wind. Bate again got through and kicking up field left the ball for Mason who outpaced everybedv and when near the line lost the ball in touch. Thie was a piece of hard luck indeed. Warrington pressed for a time, Hallam dropping fruitlessly at goal. Duckworth made another good effort before halftime when Stock- port held a lead of 8 points to 3. Saville restarted the game and Taylor returned with such ( ffect that Fleggarth had to kick dead. Deakin headed a speedy forward ruah to the home line, and from a scrimmage Duckworth made a dash, only to be held on the line. Saville kicked to the 25. but Warrington soon keturned to closer quarters. Aided by the wind Warrington seemed to have every chance, Bate being especially active and tricky. tioggarth made some fine saves in front of Warrington forwards. Isherwood essayed to cross the line after exchanges be- tween Bate and Hallam, but was • safely stooped by Saville. The visitors still held the upper hand. Duck- worth, Hallam, and Morrison passed, and the latter got over but was pulled down on his back and only a miner allowed. Saville punted out and the home forwards took play to the opposite end, Robinson following up with great dash. Morrison bad to touch Own. Bate cleared from the pack and handed the ball to Isherwood who put in a clever mu to centre. Again Warrington operated under the home goal., but the play of the three- quarters was too slow for anything,. Allen secured in his own half and handed to Worelay, who again beat Hallam and passed to Robinson, the speedy wing racing from centre behind the Warrington poste. It was a grand try and Saville had no difficulty in kicking a goal. Tee remainder of the game was almost wholly contested is the Stockport half. Bate renewed the battle on the lies, but Allen kicked out only to be penalised, Taylor making a good drop at goal. Then Robinson had an- other chance bat 'missed Wersley's pass after he had opened the field for him. Time was called soon after and Warriugton, who had hid most.of the game, were forced to accept defeat by 2 goals, 3 tries, to a try.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION. MEETING OF THE GENERAL COMMITTEE. PROFESSIONALISM ADOPTED.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION. MEETING OF THE GENERAL COMMITTEE. PROFESSIONALISM ADOPTED.

The what monthly meeting of the Committee of the above union was held in Manchester on Tuesday night, under the presidency, of Mr. J. E, Warren (Warrington), ' The matter of professionalism was again under discus- end the sub-committee's suggestions with respect to tha question were considered, and, after considerable discussion, their report was adopted, The recommenda- tions of the sub-committee are as follow :-1, That pro- fessionalism be adopted • 2, That all professional players be registered ; 3, That players must have legitimate em- ployment ; 4, That severe penalties be provided for breach of No. 3 recommendation, the club to he able to give clear proof of players following bona-fide occupations; 5, Transfer law to remain as at _ _

present, Messrs. Warren Gresty, Hutchinson, Walter, Fa.ttorini, Langshaw, and Platt were appointed a sub-committee to get out details of the scheme, and when they have ;natured such scheme to submit the same to the general committee. An application by Brig- house to present a testimonial to Hughes, one of their players, who is retiring, was ordered to remain in abey- ance. Salford made an application to be allowed to register R. Thomas, a player also claimed by the Cestla- ford club, on the ground that ho was illegally registered for that club. The committee decided that Thomas be- longs to the Castleford club. The same sut-committee as above appointed to govern the scheme of profession- ' alisrn were appainted to govern the Cup ties. There was a good representation at. the meeting, J. Houghton (St. Helens), D. F. Burnley (Batley), H. Sewell (Leeds), and J. Tatham (Liversedge) beiag the only absentees.

div.head: SPIRITUAL/SM.
div.p: SPIRITUAL/SM.

At the services of tbe Spiritualists on Sunday Miss F. Cotterill was the speaker, and in the after- noon delivered an interesting address on "A spirit's experience of passing on." In the evening the hall was crowded, and a different " control" gave a very forcible address on " Two views of the life after death," She gave clairvoyance at each meting. Monday evening's meeting was held in the Druids' Hall, and was entirely devoted to psy- chometry. Miss Cotterill gave a number of psy- chometric delineations, going very fully into details and was successful in nearly every case in obtain- ing acknowledgment of the accuracy of her state- ment.
NATIONAL INDEPRNDENT ORM= OF ODDFRLLOWS. WARRINOTON DISTRICT.

The monthly meeting of the Garibaldi Lsdge was held on Saturday, at the Little Horse Shoe Hotel, Harsemarket-street,when there was a very good at- tendance of members, including several visiting brethren,among whom were P.P.G.M. James Bram- hall, P.G. 11. Wilson, and the Grand Master of the District, William Hill, N.G. James Atkinson (in the chair),and V.T. Thomas Gregson (in the vice-chair). The balance sheet was presented by the Secretary, P.G. Thomas Dickinson, and showed the receipts to the sick and funeral fund to be £153 7s 11d, and the expenditure for sickness anu district funeral fund £ll7 12.591 The management fund has a balance of £l5 11s 2d, and the benevolent fund, £29 8s sd. The total capital worth of the lodge is £555 3s Sid, or an increase of £32 14s 2id for the year. The membership stands at 164, an increase of 28, which is considered very satisfactory. During the even- ing the late district secretary, P.P.G.M. Joseph Crosby presented P.G. Arthur A.llorne with a beau- tifully framed emblem of the Order,for services ren- dered to the lodge.

THE SALVATION ARMY. "lonel " and Mrs. Baits, assisted by " Major " and Mrs. Chandler and other officers, commenced a three days' campaign in Warrington on Saturday. A representative parch was held in the Barracks at seven o'clock on Saturday, and there was a large attendance. A reception meeting was afterwards held. On Sunday morning at seven o'clock "knee drill " was held, when tea and biscuits were pro- vided. At the Parr Hall, in the afternoon, there were about 700 present, when there was an enroll- ment of recruits who had been converted during the past month. At the night service Mrs. and " Colonel" Eadie, Mrs. and " Major " Chandler, and Mrs. Young addressed a congregation of about 1,200.---On Monday afternoon a holiness meeting was held in the Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel, and in the evening "Colonel" Eadio addressed a large audi- ence on his foreign travels.—The Rev. C. J. Millar presided. He said he knew of no society in the world that was doing the work that the Sal 'ration Army was doing. After reading the statistics as to the number of food depots, shelters, rescue homes, &c.,in connection with the Army, he said he thought it was grand, and was ju+.t the work that Jesus Christ would have them do if He had been on earth. They were caring not only for the souls but for the bodies, and that was necessary in order to secure any real permanent good. He also liked the broadness of their church. (Applause) The Salva- tion Army were the most consistent people he knew of in opposing the evil of drink. (Applause.) He was determined to fight the drink as hard as he could. Another thing he liked in the Army was that they could not muzzle it. (Laughter) There was such a thing as a golden muzzle which parsons sometimes wore. tie was thankful that he was occupying the pulpit of an unmuzzled man. They were met on a common platform, determined to do all they could to bring men and women to Christ. (Applau,.€)—" Colonel" Eadie spoke at length on his experiences in Canada and the United States and related several cases ot conversion, the address being exceedingly interesting and instruc- tive throughout.

div.head: PENTECOSTAL PENTECOSTAL LEAGUE.
div.p: THE PENTECOSTAL PENTECOSTAL LEAGUE.
MISSIOA &T WARRINGTON.

Miss E. Phillips and Miss Salter, of the Pente- costal League, commenced a special 8 days mission in Golborne-street Baptist Chapel on Sunday, when three services were held. There were large con- gregations both morning and evening, addresres being given by Miss Phillips. in the afternoon there was a Bible reading for the young. Both. ladies speak very earnestly and logically, and ranker- more pay such attention to articulation that not a word they utter is missed by their hearers. During the services on Sunday solos were sung by Miss L. Hall. Sankey's hymns have been used throughout the mission and the singing has been characterised by a spontaneity' and heartiness which is noticeable at mission services. Toe week night services in connection with the mis- sion commensed on Monday in Gslhorne-street Bipt!st Chapel, when there was a large congregation, Miss Phillips and Miss Salter occupied the pulpit with the pastor of the church, the Rev. J. T. Schofield. The ser- vice commenced with the singing of one of Ssukey'e hymns, Miss Phillips leading the congregation in an in- spiring manner. Choiuses were sung with heartiness and enthusiasm, and the lesson,which was read by Miss Phillips, was attentively listened to, her comments and explanations helping towards the comprehension of Christ's teaching. Ou Monday evening the address was given by MiSs &titer ; but before proceeding with it sh 9 explained the objects of the Pentecostal League. It was, she said,solely and simply a prayer union, in which they wha were members agreed to pray, principally for three things, in addition to praying for one another. First they prayed that God would bless every elected member; secondly they prayed that every one would be filled with the Holy Spirit ; and thirdly for spiritual holiness and the salvation of sinters. Miss Salter also pointed out that they were not another sect. They thought there were too many sects already, and tkey went in and out among the sects of the Christian Church trying to do the work God gave them in ahowiag the Christians the need or the Holy Spirit. The singins, of another hymn preceded Miss Salter'a address which' was based on the words " Sanctify in your hearts Christ as Lord," ird Peter, 15th verse. At the outset she said that no man could say "Jesus Christ is my Lord," save by the Holy Ghost. How often we heard the hymn sung "Ana crown Him Lord of all," It made her shiver to hear it sometimes, because many of the singers had not the slightest intention of crowning Him Lord of all. We let the Lord of pride rulua. Than there was money. How many of us could say that God was Lord of every peony we pos3c3sed ? The spaker thanked God that tie had at least brought her to see it and know it. We ate and &cased to please ourselves, and it was one of the great disgraces of Christianity that we lived as we did. If God was Lord of all our lives,sorne of our tables would be different and what we gave to foreign missions and home minions would be different. There were also the Lords of jealousy, malice,evil speaking, that came into our lives, and ruled and dominated us. " Sanctify in your hearts Christ as Lord !" A question which often occurred to her,said Miss Salter in con- clusion, was "Why call Me Lord and do not the things which I say ?" How dare we say that He was our Lord when he told us day after day to do this and that and we failed. God wanted our testimony and wanted us to tell other people. Before the close prayer was offered up by Miss Phillips who concluded with an earnest exhortation for evidences of leliug on the part of the congregation. In response quite three-fourths of those present stood up and uttered a few simple heartfelt words of prayer and thankful- ness.

div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
NOTES ON GA.M.ES AND
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

The penning of these notes is getting to he no light task and one which palls on the writer. Defeats ,re getting as common,and the play of the Warrington team is so rapidly deteriorating, that one's interest is undergo- ing a process of sapid evaporation.Thare was a time whea the doings of the team afforded something to comment upon favourably, and when the task of so commenting was a labour of love, but now, though there is perhaps more to talk about,the coinnaents take the nature of ad- verse criticism. This is by no means pleasant, and when Warrington accomplish something valorous, I for one, shall be as pleased as any of the growlers who express their sentiments with more force then politenesss round the home enclosure.

The Warrington Rugby Football Club is doing worse this season than last, and as far as can be seen will finish up with a considerably inferior record. Of the re- maining League matches there is only one in which Warrington may possibly secure a couple of points or even one. That is with Runcorn, the last of the visitors to Wilderspool, and it is only their shockingly bad form which makes them appear in the light of prospective sacrifices at the Warrington altar. There is aby no moans remote possibility that Warrington, ere March 12, may have played themselves into a similar state of in- efficiency as Runcorn, so that I would not give much for their chance of annexing any more points.

On Saturday they got hopelessly' snuffed " by a club which figures among the last three in the Lancashire League—Stockport to wit, and besides this they gave an exhibition which would have disgraced a third-rate club. Whenever Warrington leave their own battleground it is with their hearts in their Isoots—not their football boots even,—but their ordinary travelling boots, and their pluck in their travelling bags. Boats and bags, heart and pluck,all together remain in the dressing room when the players go forth to fight. A maximum of two away victories in a season about indicates the strength of Warrington on foreign soil.

--- Stockport had a defeat to avenge and they fulfilled their purpose to the letter. True they had little to beat, the Warrington threeqoarter line being very poor.Hallam and Morrison formed the Warrington right wing, with Moores and Isherwood on the left. In ether depart- ments the team was strong. Saville re-appeared for the home team after II weeks' absence with a broken arm. It is surprising what a lot a footballer can stand in the way of personal injuries. The Stockport captain is patched, plastered and bandaged all over, pretty nearly, and yet be goes on playing as if he were sure of a new frame when the present one is worn out. Association and Rugby are strong rivals at Stockport, and while Stockport county have had a successful season, their older Rugby neighbours have done badly, with the con- sequence that there has beeu a tramposition of gates. 3,000 would cover the numbers witnessing the Warring- ton match on Saturday. The field had a curious sur- faco,being apparently a mixture of grass,chaff,and dust, in some places to the depth of three or four inches. Occasionally when a player was bowled over he raised such a smoky cloud of dust that he became invisible for the moment and appeared to have "gone under." War- rington were far from at home in the mixture.

Of the game itself little in the way of deecription can be said. The stron4 wind spoiled what tendencies to scientific football there were, and the Warrington three- quarters sp wed what chances they had of scoring, SO that the dlsplay WAS not an edifying one. Lot me say at once that Stockport were the better team. Warrington deserved their thrashing, if only for the Awful way in which they bungled, and yet it is a fact that Stockport were defending for the biggest part of the BO minutes. The Warrington forwards and half backs were wino in,g throu4hout, but between them and the the threequarter line there was apparently no connection. Had there been anything like conabinatio n behind, Warrh gton would have won easily.

Play had not been in progress many minutes before it was plain to an onlooker who was going to be the dan- gerous man against Warrington. Moores was playing on the left wing presumably to watch Saville, while the speedy Robinson had things his own way against Hal- lain and Morrison. He very soon raced down the touch line, and would have been in but for Heesom's prompt tackle. Warrington then had a turn at attacking, but they were easily repulse i,and again the ball went out to Robinson, who this time ran right round, and scored in a good position. Then followed the sensational incident ot the match. Hardly a minute later Isherwood missed catching the ball when at full speed, over-ran it, and Davidson, a home forward, carried it over the line in a twinkling. Saville puts goal on,and Warrington seemed paralysed by their misfortune, and the chuckles of ex- ceeding delight which sounded on all sides. By dint of great exertions on the part of the front rank Warring- ton reached the home line, and Duckworth dodged over cleverly. This waa all the scoring up to leisure and lemonade.

The wind was on the Warrington side on restarting, and there seemed a good possibility of their wiping off the deficit. The homesters were sm,m penned in. but as cbanct's went a-begging one after the other my hopes be- gan to dwindle rapidly. While is this despondent frame of mind the death-blow carne. Allen and Wursley made a beautiful opening, and before you could say " Jack Robinson," one of that ilk was rpeeding off towards the Warrington end. All unopposed he scampere i and stayed not till he bad planted the oval midway between the posts, through which Saville soon propelled it. Stockport defended nearly to the close, and it was pretty to see the way in which the visitors were rolling about over the borne line. Morrison lay on his back across the rut, but the ball was above him in company with the contents of several Claret-jerseys. When the whistle sounded Smack Bate led his men off with every evidence of disgust and some blood on his countenance.

On the side of the winners Robinson was quite a hero. Both his tries Were fine efforts and gained through the slowness of the Warrington backs. Allen and Worsley worked to him very cleverly, and a fine display at full- back was given by Roggarth. It was only in the three- quarter line that Warrington were neaten. The rest; of the team were in grand form, but their efforts were wasted by the men behind. For once Isherwood and Moores were seen cempletelv off form, and with the wedkaess of the other two, the threequarter lice was a treat. Heesom played a sound game again,and at half- back I never saw Bate and Duckworth so smart and active. The forwards were all good, Taylor, Deakin, Naylor, Mason, and Barratt being ever to the fore.

To-day Warrington will be welcomed, and welcomed joyfully at Swinton. The dark blues have a painful re- collection of defeat administered only once this season, and then on the Warrington ground. Ever since they have been nursing their revenge and by now must have a fine reception prepared. Unfortunately I cannot see any chance of their conquerors,this time, making even a good fight of it. They are by no means the team they were earlier in the season,and the players chosen by the committee for the important battle appear to spell 20 points to nil of a licking all over. Eleesom is again placed on the three-quarter line. To such desperate straits are the committee forced ! The proverbial cock- roach won't be in it for slowness, and Valentine and Go. should have a rare treat in the delights of try-gottiag.
The results in the Lancashire League up to date are as follows :

*Leigh have bad two points deducted for playing an in- eligible man. The game between Wig tn and Tyldesley on Christmas Day, played at the time as a" friendly," has been ordered to stand as a Competition match.

By failing to secure a couple of points out of their match with Broughton Rangers, Swillton have consider- atny discounted their chance of finishing at the head of the Lancashire Senior Competition. With thirty-two points out of eighteen matches they are now five points behind Oldham who have, of course, played two more matches than the Swintonians. The latter also have a much stiffer list of engagements to get through than the leaders, and present appearances porit strongly to Old- ham at last reaching the semmit of toeir desire. Both Widnes and Broughton Rangers are well in the running for third plea., and their meeting ttis week end should prove a great attraction in the chemical district. St. Helens got a further couple of points at the expense of Leigh, theugh the latter were somewhat unfortunate. Apparently realising their danger of becoming wooden spoonista Rochdale Hornets made no mistake in their encounter with Tyldesley, meantime Morecambe could only manage t 4 draw with Runcorn,whose degeneration is unfortunately maintained.

OUR NEW STORY. HAVE MUCH PLEASURE IN ANNOUNCING THAT WE HAVE ARRANGED FOR THE PUBLICATION OF A • ••• •••ivr EW SERIAL STORY ENTITLED " THE WHEEL OF FATE." IN OUR COLUMNS, COMMENCING ON FEBRUARY 12Ta. WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL --- The monthly meeting of the above Council was held in Bewaey.street Chambers on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. W. Houghton presideu, and there were also present, Messrs. R. T. Lawe, J. Dignum, J. Ball, T. Halton, J. Johnson, J. W. Knowles, S. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (surveyor), and J. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector). FINANCE. The CLERK reported that the balance in the hands of the treasurer on the General account was £355 17s. 11d. and on the Burtonwood Sewerage account £1,052 2310 d THE SANITARY INSPECTOR'S WORK. The CLERK reported that Mr. Bryden, Chief Inspector of Canal Boats, had paid his usual visit to the district and expressed himself as very well satisfied with the work of the Inspector, and added that he had not yet come to a district where the work was better performed. WATER AT HERMITAHE GREEN. With reference to the water supply at Hermitage Green the Clerk said that the water rates would amount to £lO 3s. 10d. showing a deficiency of £2l '163. 2d. on the per centage of the capital outlay, which would have to be made up from the general rate. Mr. Widdows re- quired a water supply and the cost of laying.lt would be £434 16s. 7d., for a 6 inch main. Mr. BALL said the deficiency would mean a rate of nearly ltd. in the £. Be objected to a supply being put down. Mr. J. W. Knowles thought that the two cottages put up by Mr. Widdows could be supplied from the well ' which supplied the other cottages. Mr. Widdows appeared before the Council and after some discussion the matter was left over to the next meeting, Mr. Widdows in the meanwhile coming to a de- cision whether to pay a portion of the capital outlay for putting down a water supply. A COMPLAINT FROM PENKETH. Mr. DIONUM mentioned that the water supply to seven cottages in Penketla-lane was at times bad. Sit of the tenants refused to drink it and ene of them had com- plained to him about it. The Cmtnx said the water had been certified to be good by the analyst. Mr. DIGNUM said that in dry weather the water was good, but in rainy weather it was bad. The CiammaN suggested that the Ispector should take another sample during the wet weather and have the water again analysed. The INSPECTOR said he would see Mr, Rogers,the land- lord,and see if he would put a supply in from the mains. —The matter was left in the hands of the Inspector for a month. DUST CONTRACT. Mr. DIGNUM moved and Mr. LOWE seconded that Mr. Pownall be allowed £lO per annum increase on his con- tract for the removal of night-soil in Penketh.—The In- specter said that he thought Mr. Pownall required an extra £lO as the work v as heavy. REPORTS. The SURVEYOR reported that the following plans had been submitted and might be approved :—Mr. T. H. A. Pilkington' 9 cottages,: Winwick-road, Longford ; Mr. N. McGuire, 2 houses, Manchester-road, Poulton-srith- rearnhead; Messrs.Rigby and Mason, 12 cottages, Penny- lane, Collins Green. The report was adopted, together with that of the Inspector. This was all the business.

_ INDEPENDENT LABOUR PARTY, Mr. John Edwards, president of the Liverpool Fabian Society, gave an address under the Adepieell of the above at the weekly meeting, held in the Druids' Hall on Sunday evening, entitled" Freedom and Industrial Slavery." He traced the growth and progress of the present political power possessed by the people, showin the work done and persecution by our forefathers during the agitn. tion for our present political advantages. Compar tively we were more politically free than in a- r European country; but political freedom and power unless used effectively, did not bring industriel freedom. The essential of slavery was the depen- dence of one man upon another for the means of life. Under our pre•ent commercial system th. workers were industrial slaves ; for except by the wish or desire of the capitalist, employer and land• lord, to employ them they were denied the right to work and consequently the right to live.
